CHINA.

[FOURTII ARTICLE.]

IT was supposed and boldly prophesied by
the advocates of tho aggressive and violent
policy, that when live Chinese ports had been
opened to British manufactures, that our trade
with China would increase rapidly, and that
wealth and, prosperity would accrue to :the
English industrial classes. But the prophets
were Wrong. In 1854, our exports to China
Were leas than in 1835,- though the smuggling
trade of opium from India into China had
increased. This fact was -demonstrated by
COBDEN in the debate on Chine, May 31st,
1804, in which he shows that our Chinese
policy had failed commercially—that although
the trade increased a little after each fresh
opening out of markets, this increase did not
continue, but on the contrary the trade always
fell back more than it had advanced.. And
before the evente had occurred to whichl ata
coming, the English Government was in the
possession of compl‘te information and
evidence, which showed how erroneous had
been the political and: eommercial views as to
the result of Chinese trade; bow different the
civilisation and industrial organisation of
China was to that of Europe ; how hopeless
it was to attempt by force to change their
customs and modes of life, and that the only
possible way in which our trade could be
developed, lay in pursuing a legitimate, peace-
able, and moral policy, in treating with the
Chinese upon a footing of equality by just
barter and by honourable dealing. In another
column of this number of the BKE-litvn will
be found an account of Chinese industry taken
from a memorandum by Mr. Namur. .on
the Chinesetrade; and it is well Worth reading.
In the face of such facts as he there describes,
and which were fully confirmed by other
evidence, the English Government .still clung
to its baleful policy—a policy which, after these
facts were known, cannot be palliated by the
excuse Of ignorance.. The Government
resolved to force the Chinese trade. 'War
was the certain consequence of that resolu-
tion, The Chinese were to be forced to trade
against their will; and they could only be
forced by war. The industrious classes,
according to Lord PALMERSTON, Who-
produce British coinmodities, were to
be made happy and prosperous at home. And
war was to be made upon 300 millions of
peaceable industrious men. The smallest
grievances, the slightest incivilities of the
Chinese to the English were collected together
and cherished as wrongs. A blue book ap-
peared in 1857, entitled Insults in China ; ".
and in that same year the first opportunity
that presented itself was seized, and We went
to war to avenge the taliing of a pirate ship
by the Chinese Government. One most
im-
portant element in the circumstances which
preceded and led to this vox, was the tate of
the Island of Hong Kong, which bad been
ceded to. England by .the Treaty of Nankin.
During the whole of the time since we have.
'held Mug Kong, the condition of things.
there 11,1. s been a disgvaeo to England, and to
the civil Led World. I eannut enter at length

into this. I advise those who want to under-
stand fully the iniquity of this war, to read
Dr. BRIDGES' historical account of these
doings at Hong Kong in his admirable article
upon China in "International Policy." He
shows that it was a nest of smugglers, pirates,
and robbers. He unravels the intrioato net-
work of a most astounding conspiracy between
the English and the pirates, whereby the
latter were enabled, under the protection of
the British flag, to ravage the Chinese seas
with perfect impunity. He shows, in one
word, that Hong Kong, under British rule,
was a noxious ulcer in Chinese social exist-
ence. lam told that it is now a collection of
all that is worst and wickedest in those parts
of the earth. The last thing we have heard.
of is the existence of gambling hells, sane
tioned by the Hong Kong officials. From this
den of wickedness and piracy the ship, Arrow
had gone cruising. She was Chinese built.
Her owner and her crew were Chinese subjects,
though her master, who was not on board
when the ship and crew were seized by the
Chinese authorities, was a British subject.
Even' Sir JOIN BOWItING, the Governor of
Hong Kong, says, "It appears that the Arrow
had no right to hoist the British flag; the
license to do so 'expired on the 27th of Sep-
tember, from which period she has not been
entitled to protection." Politicians and rhe-
toricians know well how to disguise facts like
these, with specious arguments and beautiful
phrases. But this occurrence was a mere
pretext, which wry! eagerly seized upon as the
excuse for extending our trade by means of
war. Indeed, our statesmen openly avowed
that such was their policy, while they went to
war to avenge the suppression, by the Chinese
Government, of piracy, of which Hong Kong
was the focus.

Troops were sent out with Lord ELGIN in
1857. But the Indian Mutiny broke out, and
they were sent to India instead. In December
of the same year, warlike operations were
commenced, which ended in the—TreatY, of
Tien-tsin in the summer of 1858. - ',Ord
ELotlr returned to England, and the final
settlement Of the Treaty was to take place in
June, 189, at the apito.l, at Pekin. Mr
Butlen was authorised to to to Tien-tsin in a
man-of-war, and thence to proceed to Pekin
The Chinese officials met him at Shanghai,
and desired to disauss several matters respect-
ing the Treaty. Mr. BRUCE thinking that they
wanted to gain time, and meant to oppose his
passage up the :Mho River to Pekin, resolved
to force a passage. Just before ho begin, he
was informed that a diffeient route bad been
arranged for his journey to Pekin. Not satis-
fied with this, he proceeded to carry out his
resolution, and to force his way up the river.
He ; attacked the Tahoe forts at the mouth of
the river, and met with a severe repulse.
Here was a manifest aggression on our part.
The Chinese had not undertaken in the Tien-
tsin Treaty that the route up the Peiho River
to Pekin should be open, .and ;they Will en -
titled to require our ambassador to go by any ;
route they might choose to indicate. In fact, it
was not desirable that an English Man-of-war
PhOUiti go up the river, Nevertheless, the
English Government regarded this repulse at
the Takeo forts as a declaration of war. Lord
&ow was sent out with a considerable force
in 1860, and was completely auecessful. The
war WM vigorously and promptly brought to
a close. in October of the same year, to avenge
the alleged violation of a flag of truce, and
the impriaonment of somnEnglishmen by the
Chinese general, the summer palace of the
Emperor, one of the most beautiful works of
art in China, was burnt and plundered by the
British, and French troops—a gross and
wanton act of Vandalism, done not in despair
and .the agony of defeat, but deliberately by.
the antherityof those in command; as a kind
of ,reprisal.

The Treaty of Tient-tsin was then ratified.
Its terms were briefly confirmation of the
Treaty (kf Nankin, in An ambassador
to reside at Pekin. Five additional ports
to be opened, besides the navigation of
the Vang-tse itiver, and three place on the
river. The right of exterritorialitv was ex-
torted—that is, "13HO-till subjects who may
commit any crime in China Shall be tried and
puniahed by the Consul, or other publio

tionary authorised 'thereto, according to the
laws of Great Britain." "A. British subject,
having reason to complain of a Chinese, must
proceed to. the Consulate and state his
grievance. The Consul will inquire into the
merits of the case, and will do his utmost to
arrange it amicably. In like manner, if a
Chinese haie reason to complain of a British
subject, the Consul shall no less listen to his
complaint, and endeavour to settle it in tt.
friendly manner." (Articles xvi., xvii.) The
Treaty further compelled certain transit duties,
imposed on produce as it passed from one
province to another, to be commuted for a
fixed payment. The introduction of opium
at a fixed duty was legalised. The duty was
fixed by Lord ELGIN against the wishes of the
Chinese Government. And lastly, an indem-
nity was to be paid by the province of Can-
ton to England for the expenses of the war.
To conclude, we have waged a series of the
most unjustifiable wars, with the avowed
policy of forcing trade upon China. On
different occasions we have made them pay a
war indemnity, a proceeding which is in itself
a violation of international law, and whieh
example Prussia has lately followed. We
have compelled them to open their ports to us,
and to trade with us. We have regulated
their internal commercial affitirs against their
will. We have seized the island of Hong
Kong, which, owing to our misgovernment,
has become a nuisance of the most serious
description. We have compelled them to
open the great Yang-tse river to our ships, as
to which Sir F. BRUCE, in writing in 1863 to
Earl RUSSELL, speaks of the "constant scenes
of blood and violence which have inaugurated
the opening of the Yang.tse river." We
compel the Chinese to submit to our courts of
justice and refuse to recognise those of the
Chinese. Lastly, we have not only prevented
the Chinese. Government from carrying out
their great sanitary scheme of putting down
the sale of opium in China, as it has been
successfully put down in Japan, but we have
forced them to legalise the trade. ,

Such is a brief account of our doings in
China, which I believe I have understated,
and certainly not exaggerated. What wonder
if the Chinese should dislike and distrust us.
For my own part, I have no words with which
I Can express the depth of shame and humilia-
tion which I feel when I consider England's
conduct to the people of China. Next week I
shall write on the Opihnt debate.

CluEsnoN.--In what way is the knowledge
of the causes of evil and of good to man so

of character as you state it to be? And how
is the want of this knowledge so extremely
influential for evil ? And, what are the er-
roneous ideas upon this subject which are so
extremely injurious ?
ANSWEIL—The leading erroneous idea
which men have in the absence of the know-
ledge of causes, and which they could not have
if they had this knowledge, is the supposition
that individual roan is himself the primary
cause of his qualities (or character), and of
his opinions and determinations, and conse-
quently of his acts. In this supposition,
which is the common idea of free will, there
are two parts. There is a true part, which is
the assertion of the highly important truth—
the basis of man's moral respon.,ihility—
That man is an agent, an native cause, in
the forming of his character, opinions, and
determinations; or that he has and, exercises
a power or self-education and self-govern-
ment.

And there is an erroneous part, which is
016 denial of the truth which is the basis of
the knowledge of the causes of evil and of
good to man—the denial of the truth,
Tbat mu is vausod to acquire the character
which he does acquire, aid tQ rum the

ions and determinations whioh he does form;
or that he is the creature of causation—that
he iq caused to exercise his powers us he doe s
exercise them. •

To imagine that man is himself the primary
cause of his character, &c., is of course to be
ignorant of this second truth, and to deny it.
And the denial of this truth, in the erroneous
part of the common idea of free will, is the
fundamental error of. the old, system, and, is
the fundamental pr primary cause of evil to
man. And it is so in this manner. While
men imagine that each individual is the pri-
mary cause of his character and conduct, &c.,
they are caused by this ignorant and false idea
to blame and punish with unkindness, and
in many eases with bitterness, vindictive-
ness, and cruelty, those who are or do
what is displeasing to them. And the
ignorant, and falsely based, and, .unkind
feelings and acts which are thus produced (or
caused to occur), and, the blindness to the
effects of these feelings and proceedings, and to
their causes, which is thus (caused to be)
perpetuated, are productive of very deterio-
rating effects upon the intellect and the moral
nature of ,those who thus ignorantly and
harshly blame, and unkindly and unjustly
treat their fellow beings, and of those
who are thus ignorantly, and un-
kindly, and. unjustly treated. And as,
while men arc thus in error and intellectually
blind, no means—intellectual, moral, or
material—can be intelligently adopted to
remove the causes of evil, and especially the
primary cause, the evil effects are continually
reproduced; the unkindness and harshness are
ontinually caused to be repeated, in various
ways; and blamers and blamed, punishers and
punished, are constantly experiencing the con-
sequent process of intellectual and moral
deterioration. • And the ramifications of moral
and physical evil which are thus produced are
interminable.

We may 'thus trace to this funchmental
cause of evil to this fundamenta
error—all the injurious passions, and all the
disunion and mutual opposition, and. all
the injustice, and all the deception, and all
the superstition and folly, and all the injurious
proceedings, and all the injurious material
surroundings formed by man, which now
occur or exist, and all the annoyances and
miseries, small and great, which are produced
by these secondary causes of evil. If DIM
were so far enlightened as to know the causes o
evil and of good to the human race, they would
no longer be superstitious; the causes of evil

withdrawn ; and the causes of good feelings

which would be in the highest degree con-
ducive to the happiness 'of all, would be
substituted for them. For the fundamental
error which ía the fundamentaLeause of evil to
man oan he mote exist in those by whom the
causes of evil and of good to man are known,
than darkness can cover the earth when the
sun is shining. And when the cause is
removed, its effects will die away in due time,
as a plant perishes when its root is cut off.
And in this Case there will be not only the
cutting off of the root of the tree of evil, but
also the setting of the root of the tree of good
in its place.
And the idea that each individual is the
primary cause of his (totalities, &e., is a most
effectual harrier, while it is retaiued, to the
discovery that it is this idea which is the
primary cause of all these evils. And it is for
this reason. that the endeavours of men for the
removal of moral evil have hitherto been limited
to attempts to influence individuals by precepts
and exhortations, and threats and promises,
and punishments and reward, and by other
superficial external means, and that the
success of this course of action has been
extremely limited. For such proceedings are
no more than endeavours to modify the effects
of the primary cause of evil, and of secondary
causes of evil consequent upon it. And, of
course, so long as the causes continue in
existence their effects will continue to be
produced in defiance of all such ignorant and
superficial proceedings. And, as already
stated, the effects of these proceedings are in
many respects highly injurious. But no other
means can be adopted by persona who are

ignorant and in error in reference to the

influence of the erroneous idea which is the
primary cause,of 'evil, and under the influence
of the injurious habits of thought, and
feeling, and action, which are the effects

These are facts, which every intelligent
person may ascertain for himself, when they
are pointed out, if he will take notice of what
is constantly occurring within him and around
him—if he will trace, upon these points, the

which he may observe in his own internal
experiences, and in others. It is only because

of observation that they at first dnd dififoultY

When man knows the causes of evil and of

and material influences by which the indi-
viduals have been caused to be mentally

qualities. And ho will know that justice,
combined with sympathy, requires that he
should be sorry for the individuals who have
been caused to become bad, and that he should
feel kindly towards , them, and that in
blaming them he should always remember that
they were not themselves the primary cause of
their badness. And he will know that the
causes of good must be substituted for the

expectation that evil effects will cease to be

articles.text:
TRADES INTELLIGENCE
AND LABOUR NEWS.
[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENTS.]

LONDON.

TELE BUILDERS AND TILE NINE MUMS' MOVEMENT.

_
The London builders, at a meeting on Thursday,
determined to adhere to their published resolution,
and have notified the fact to both tho operative
masons and carpenters and joiners.

NORTHAMPTON.
THE ceurErrnts AND JOINERS.

A meeting of carpenters and joiners has been held
for the purpose of taking steps to ask the masters to
concede the nine hours' movement, and to adopt a
now code of rules for the governance of those
trades. Tho meeting was well attended, and was
presided over by Mr. Pickering. There were also
present Mr. E. Brimley and Mr. G. Pell, dele-
gates from the amalgamated carpenters and
joiners' society, *and Mr. Thompkins and Mr.
Green, &legates from the local society; the four
forming delegates from the trades' council. The
chairman denounced strikes as injurious to both
employer and employed, and referred to the
general concession of the nine-hour movement
in all parts of the country. He advocated the
principle of uniformity of labour, especially in the
building trade, and requested the meeting to
pass the rules Which would be submitted to them,
The rules were passed, and the Ist of April Was
fixed upon as the day on which it should be sug-
gested that these rules come into operation.

BRISTOL.
TILE MASONS AND TIIEID, E3IPLOYEIIB.

r At Bristol, the adjourned interview between the
operative masons and their employers took place on
Thursday last, Mr. J. Foster, presiding. Since
the last meeting the masons' society had discussed
the suggestions- made by the employers, and the
deputation now informed the employers present
that the society had agreed to all the proposals
made by the masters excepting the worked stone
rule and payment by the hour: the latter, how-
eier,•.somaof the men present believed, would soon
be more .favourably considered., One of them
said that, he had, up to: within
,the last week or
so, worked in London under the hour system, and
he, although at one time as much opposed to the
system as anyone, found no fault with it, but,
on'the contrary, believed it to be the best plan for
both employers and employed. A meeting of the
employers connected with the local association
and the trade generally will shortly be called, to
consider the report of the sub-committee of em-
ployers and association and to consider the notices
emanating from the carpenters and joiners.

OXFORD..
STRIKE OF CARPENTERS..

About 500 building operatives struck work in
the city of Oxford on Monday morning on the
question of tile nine-hour day. The demand of
the men was last week met by an offer from the
masters to make 56i hours the week's work, and
to further consider the question when the
movement became more general. At a meeting
held on Thursday evening, Professor Thorold
Itnexs in the chair, this offer was rejected, and a
resolution adopted to strike if the whole of the
40mand were net conceded. At a meeting of the
masters on Saturday a resolution was come to
offering to receive a deputation of one man from
each firm, and promising to treat their repre-
sentations with respect and consideration. This
resolution was placed before a meeting of the
Operatives held in the open air in front of the City
Gaol on Monday morning, but rejected, and a
resolution was passed to keep out for a month.

LEEK.
LOCK OUT IN Tra: LEEK SILK TRADE.

The whole of the mills in the town of Leek were
locked on Saturday, and all operations are sus-
pended. This action has been taken in consequence
of what the masters consider the exorbitant de-
mands of the men. Several of the operatives at
once left the town for the purpose of seeking work
in Macclesfield or Congleton. At a meeting of the
Masters' Committee it was unanimously resolved
to communicate by circular with the clients of the
various firms, infortuing them of the state of
affairs in the town, and asking them not to feel
aggrieved at the inconvenience of not having their
orders complied with, as the masters were unani-
mously resolved to resist the men's demands.

GLASGOW.
MEETING OF GLASGOW MINERS.

A general meeting of the coal miners in the
Glasgow district was held on Saturday. Reports
Were given in from the various works to the effect
that tome of the pita wero waking on short time
itnti get All were Idle fer the meeting;

Mr. M`Donald addressed the men. lie alluded
to the success which had attended the eight hours
movement in Fife and other places, and urged the
Glasgow men to unite and agitate for a restriction
of labour and shorter time; and if this were done
effectually the wages would in a short time rise.
After a good deal of discussion resolutions were
then adopted that every man commence to restrict
his labour to the value of 53. per day, and that
each work send a deputation to the employer, re-
questing that the men be allowed to go down the
pit at 6 a.m., and stop at 3 p.m., with one hour for
meals; and to stop at 1 p.m. on Saturdays. The
desire was expressed to have the hours sltertened
in the morning, and that the men should not enter
the pit earlier than six o'clock—the practice at
present being to go down the pit between 4 and 5
o'clock in the morning.

articles.title: BIRMINGHAM.
articles.text:
BIRMINGHAM.

TILE NUT AND BOLT lIIKEIIS. STRIKE.

On Saturday night a meeting of working men
was held at the Public Office, Moor-street, to ex-
press sympathy with the men on strike in the above
trade. Mr. Gilliver (secretary of the Birmingham
Trades Council) prosi ded, in the absence of the
Rev. A. O'Neil. Mr. Juggins (secretary of the
Darlaston Nut and Bolt Makers' Society) addressed
the meeting at considerable length upon the
objects sought by the men, and the best way of
obtaining what they wore striving for. He urged
the desirability of unity of action, propriety of
conduct, and determination, and expressed a belief
that throughout the whole of the district the men
were determined not to surrender until the masters
met them fairly in their demands. Mr. Radford
and other gentlemen having spoken, it was decided
that the men should remain on strike, and a sub-
scription fund was commenced in aid of the men.

THE WIIIPMAKERS.

On Tuesday night a well-attended meeting of
operatives of the above trade was held at the
White Horse, Lower Essex-street, to discuss the
question of the advance of 10 per cont, on their
present rate of wages, resolved upon at a previous
meeting. Mr. J. Lovell occupied the chair. The
Secretary (Mr. Newton) announced that two of
the leading firms had consented to give an advance
of ô per cent., unconditionally, and for a perma-
nency After some discussion, it was proposed
that the offer be accepted throughout tbo trade.
The motion met with some disapprobation, and on
being put to the meeting was lost, and the original
resolution of 10 per cent., to commence on the
18th inst., was carried.

articles.title: LEEDS. TUE STRIKEI.
articles.text:
LEEDS.
TUE STRIKEI.

A rumour was in circulation on Tuesday morn-
ing that Mr. Tennant, of 'Hives and Tennant, had
requested all the men to meet him at two o'clock,
but the delegates who acted upon the rumour,
ascertained it to be without foundation. It was
subsequently resolved that communications from
the various masters should only be received
through the central ,committee. The hands
employed by Messrs. Patterson of Meadow-lane
resumed their employment on Tuesday morning
on the nine hours' system, the firm, towards the
end of last Week, having intimated their readi-
nees to make the concession. Thorn is nothing
new to state with regard- to the rest of the firms.
It is stated by the representatives of the men that
in Leeds and the district the men employed in
other trades have subscribed very liberally towards
the support of the hands on strike, and intima-
tion has been received that in the course of a day
or two subscriptions will ho forwarded from places
et a distance. The number of persons on strike
is believed not to be so largo as was estimated
last week. On Wednesday the allowance resolved
to be given to the turn-outs by the central com-
mittee was distributed. It is said that many of
those who struck work have obtaiapd employment
in other trades, and in connection with this matter,
we may mention a report—for its truth we cannot
vouch—that in one instance a man had obtained
employment, but As as dismissed upon the receipt
of a letter from one of the masters stating that he
was a strike hand.

TICE STRIKES IN' TICE FLAX, rELT, AND CLOTH

TRADES.

There is no change to note in the position of the
strike in the flax trade. The hands continue to
absent themselves from the mills, and appear de.
terniined to stand by their conic firmly, Support
has begun to conic in liberally, many of the work-
people in Leeds and in other towns having re-
solved to make weekly contributions. Delegates
have been despatched to different parts of the
country, with the object of arousing sympathy and
securing assistance. At the last interview(
of the men with the masters, it appears
that the masters *did intimate their decision
on au) question ;—namely, that they would not)

without a reduction of wages, reduce the hours
from 58i to 54 per week. They promised to lay
the case of the men before other employers in the
trade, but did not bind themselves to give any
further answer.

Since the above was in print, the following
circular has been published by the operatives,
headed,

A.rrsAL TO TUB PUBLIC IN OBI:BUIL.

We, the operatives now on strike for the nine
houro, solicit your subscriptions to aid us in ob-
taining the same. We have appealed to our em-
ployers for the concession, and they have refused
the same. We think it right that we should
endeavour to obtain for women and children
as short working hours as Able-bodied men now
possess. ,

We also believe that our masters can really
afford the concession asked for, seeing that
machinery has increased 70 per cent., while labour
has only increased 40 per cent. since the passing of
the Ten Hours' Act.

We hope you will kindly assist us in this struggle,
it being admitted that we are in Flax Mills the
poorest paid of all factory operatives.
All contributions, and letters will be thankfully
received, addressed to Mr. Morris, secretary, at the
Central Committee Room, Old Assembly Rooms,
Leeds.

P. 0.0. made payable to James Kirk, Treasurer.
By order of the committee.

The committee of the operatives on strike re-
ceived a communication from Mr. Patterson,
Meadow-lane, in which he agrees to the nine
hours' limit, and asks his bands t o return to work.
The committee have complied with Mr. Patter-
son's request, and work was resumed in his mill on
Monday morning.
THURSDAY EVENING.—There is nothing new to
report as to the position of affairs between the
employers and the workmen who are on strike for
shortei hours. The hands in the flax trade, who
have been out since Monday week, received their
"first strike pay" yesterday afternoon. The total
sum at the disposal of the committee, received from
Leeds alone, was £270, which was distributed as
follows :—llalf-timers, 4d. each ; 6s. a week hands,
Od. each; over Gs. and under 10s., Is. 41. each.
The men received no pay. The total number
relieved was close upon 5,000. The hands were
paid at places near their respective mills, at
different times of the day, each overlooker calling
the names of those who had been employed under
him. A large number of hands are said to have
left the town, having secured employment in other
places.

articles.title: FELT TRADE.
articles.text:
THE FELT TRADE.

A week Ago the operatives in the felt trade in
Leeds, of whom there are probably not more than
500 employed, gave notice that they required a
reduction of working hours to 54 per week. The
notice terminated on Saturday, and, the masters
not complying, a strike has taken place in connec-
tion with the two principal firms—Messrs. Wil-
kinson, of Ilunalet, who employ about 200, and
the Patent Woollen Cloth Company, Elmwood
Mills, Camp-road, who employ about 230 hands.
A third firm, that of Carr awl Butterworth, Lady
Pit-lane, has agreed to reduce the hours as re-
quired on the 13th of April, and in this instance
no strike has occurred. Tiiess are the leading
firms in the trade.

A numerously attended meeting of the hands
who have struck work was • held on Srturday
evening at the Red Lion, Meadow-lane, and was
presided over by Mr: Win. Holmes. The follow-
ing resolution was agreed to unanimously, on the
proposition of Mr. W. MoTuatt, seconded b y
Mr. S. Shott :—" That, in the opinion of this
meeting, the working of 513 f hours per week by
the hardeners, willeyers, fettlers, and women
tillers, and all workers in connection with the felt
mills, is too long, and that they should be reduced
to ,51 per week ; and that this meeting pledges
itself not to go back to the mills again until the
nine hours system is conceded by the masters."

articles.title: CLOTH TRADE.
articles.text:
THE CLOTH TRADE.

A meeting of the ,cloth-finishing operatives was
held on Saturday evening in the Assenably-rooms,
for the purpose of ascertaining how many firms
are working on the nine hours s 3 stem. The
meeting was well attended. The names of all
the firms were called over, and it then appeared
that 41 have made the concession ; that only
three, whose hands arc on sinks, have refused it;
and that two are waiting the result of the strike
in connection with the three. The three firms
are those of Howden and Wade, Padgett, and
Webster; the two—Hargreaves and Nussey, and
Pawson. The following resolution was carried
unanimously with reSpeet to overtime :—" That
all overtime be paid at the rate of time and a
quarter to eight o'clock; after that time up to
twelve; time and a half; aft vr twelve o'clock,

double time." It was agreed to appoint six men
to wait upon the same number of masters to settle
this question.

Messrs. Marshall and Co. have issued the fol-
lowing notice to their workpeople
The step which you have taken in going out on
strike -without giving your employers notice of
your intention, and without seeking any rational
means of discussing fully and temperately with us
the claim which has beers made for a reduction
of the hours of work, will result in loss to us,
and both loss and hardship to yourselves.

We will now state shortly the reasons why we
cannot accede to your request and adopt the nine
hours time.

1. We do not consider the present hours of
labour established by Act of Parliament, or those
worked in our mills, excessive or injurious to
women and children, considering the lightness of
their work. We believe that independent and
satisfactory evidence to this effect may be pre.
duced. It must be remembered that on the
Continent the same class of hands work 72 hours
a week, and even more. The limit of 64 hours
per week has been chiefly applied to the more
laborious work of men; and in very many cases
the men, without hardship, work much longer
hours.

2. The proposed reduction of time would cause
the employers a heavier loss than the condition of
their trade will bear, both from the diminished
production of their machinery and capital, and
especially considering the claim that the wages to
be received by the workpeople are to remain at
their present amount.

3. The reduced number of flax spinners in
Leeds (more than 20 firms having failed, or re-
tired, since 1837) shows the diculty o competing
with Ireland and Scotland, and with the mills
on the Continent, which last, working from 72 to
as much as 84 hours per week, are not only com-
peting with us with increasing success in foreign
markets, but are even selling large quantities of
yarn in the home markets, and supplanting us in
the trade of our own country.

4. These considerations show that the proposed
shortening of hours of labour is not called for, and
would be attended with serious loss to the em-
ployers, and great danger to the flax trade in
Leeds, in which the workpeople are as much in-
terested as the employers.

These are the reasons for which we refused the
demand for the concession of nine hours' labour
without reduction of wages, and for which we
declined to withdraw our refusal when we met
the deputation on Friday last.

articles.text:
WARWICKSHIRE.

STJtHU 01,

A meeting of landowners and tenant formers,
representing the wholo of the agricultural interest
in South Warwickshire, was held at Wellesbourne,
on Tuesday, Sir Charles aorgan, Part., presiding,
to resist the strike of farm lahourers, which vcnn.
menced
on mond,y, aad threatens to extend
through the whole division. There were upwards
of luU of the leading agriculturists prosout. Thu
followiag resolutions were unanimously adopted :
" 1. That this meeting most earnestly deprecates
any combination amongst labourers which
originates or fosters discord or disruption between
tho agricultural labourers and their employers. 2.
That this meeting is most anxious t%) preserve intact,
feelings of goodwill and confidence which bave.for
the most pal prtrrttiled hetween the above cittssoc:

3. That this meeting is firmly convinced that in the

ally union against their employers, to persuade

That this meeting considers the demands already

articles.title: SOUTH STAFFORDSHIRE. TUTE M 11411103.
articles.text:
SOUTH STAFFORDSHIRE.
TUTE M 11411103.

On Tuesday night a meeting of miners of
the Wednesbury, West Bromwich, and surround-
ing districts was held at the Three Crowns Inn,
Hill Top, on the question of the nine hours'
movement, and to bring under the notice of the
men the advantages that would arise by the
passing of the Mines Regulation Bill.
The Chairman, in opening the meeting, alluded
to the evils that beset the miners in times past,
some of which had been overcome. Ito particu-
larly instanced the " torarny shop" system, which
had hitherto been such a bane to them. Coming
down to the present day, he acknowledged that
the "bandsmen" had been wonderfully benefited
by the recent concession of the masters; but at
the same time that concession was not sufficiently
complete to thoroughly satisfy the colliers, who
wore as much entitled to have the nine hours
allowed to them on every day of the week as any
other class of workers, lie enforced the absolute
necessity of thorough organisation during the
preterit crisis; and the only real and substantial
way of becoming consolidated as one body was by
recourse to unionism.

Mr. Thomas Griffiths apologised for the ab-
sence of Mr. Thomas Halliday (president of the
Amalgamated Miners' Association) and Mr Brown;
who bad promised to be present. He hoped
that when they did come they% would bring with
them petitions (for the men to sign) in favour of
the Mines Regulation Bill which was at present
before Parliament. It was, he continued, the best
bill that was ever brought before Parliament;
and they would corroborate him in this state-
ment when they had the opportunity of reading
it themselves. It would prevent the occurrence
of so many accidents that had, for many years,
hazarded the life of the miner; it would provide
the men against working in a sulphurous atmos-
phere or in the deadly "choke damp ;" it would
do away with the excuse for " fences ;" and it
would render the managers of pits liable to prose-
cution if they failed to comply with any of the
regulations of the bill. (Applause.) The masters,
It would appear, were bringing all their power
to bear in opposing its passing ; but he was glad
to say that there were men in the House of
Commons who were determined that the Bill
should pass. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Mime (the
Home Secretary) had introduced the bill, and
he had every hope that it would pass the Com-
mons. When it was passed it would necessitate
the keeping of a register at every colliery
showing the state of the pit. It would also do
away with the pernicious system of paying by
the " totmuy shop" plan. Referring to the
present agitation, the speaker said it was to his
mind a shameful thing that they had not long
before this participated in the nine hours system.
("And it is ".) The men had been blamed for
'the present increase in the price of coal. It was
the fault of the masters that this state of thieg,s
was produced. (Hoar, hoar.) If the workmen
bad not asked for the concession of even a minute
in their hours of labour, or a penny in their
wages, the masters would have demanded jus
the same prices. (" So they would ".) The
masters were obtaining a high price for the con
from the public, but the getter of that coal was
not asking for a small share of it. They were
entitled to an extra pay of Is. 6d. per day and a
reduction to nine hours every day. (Much
applause.) The price of coal was increased in 1861
and 1863 3s. per ton, and the wages rose is. 6d.
Since that time coal had risen 48., and the
masters having taken off the "overweight" (equi-
valent to is.), made a rise of ss. They were,
therefore, arguing by the previous grant,
clearly entitled to 2s. 6d. Granting that
they obtained a reduction to nine hours per day, it
would be equivalent to giving the men is.; and
after that they would perceive they ought to got
is. 6d. per day. Having combatted the many
assertions as to the neglect of the men in attending
to their work, Mr, Griffith/0R thht tho time had

come when they ought to demand their rights
("And it has") ; they ought therefore to take
advantage of it. (Applause.) A Miner, in the
body of the room, said the men did not want any
more wages; they only wanted a reduction of the
hours of labour; they had plenty of wages. Mr.
Griffiths explained that he did not want it to be
inferred that the man were striking for an increase
of wages; but what he did wish to be understood
was that if the masters forced them to strike (by
not granting the reduction in the working hours)
they would not strike for nothing; they would
make it the instrument of getting an advance in
their pay. (Applause.)
A Collier believed that on Saturday next the
masters would yield the point, and allow the men
to go to work en the nine hours' system. (Hear,
hear.)
A resolution having been passed pledging the
men to remain out until they obtained their
demands, the meeting closed.

articles.text:
HULL.

TRE CORDWAINERS.

A meeting was held on Monday morning of
the Hull branch of the Amalgamated Shoemakers'
Society, to receive the report of the deputation
appointed to wait upon the masters for their
answer to the memorial sent to them a week ago
asking for an advance on the present rate of wages.
The secretary was happy to say that the em-
ployers, with one exception, had received them in
a gentlemanly manner, and they had agreed to
give the advance agked for in it friendly spirit, one
master saying they deserved credit for the modera-
tion of their request. Mr P. W. Milner moved,
and Mr E. Cahill seconded the following resolu-
tion:—" That the best thanks of this meeting be
given to the masters for the courteous manner
they have received the deputation, and the generoys
way they have given tho advance asked," The
resolution was carried with three cheers.

CAISTOR.
LABOUR AND WAOEM.

On Saturday evening the second meeting of
labourers was held in a barn at the George Inn
yard. A miner presided, and R. Coulbeck miner
Thomas Moore, marine store dealer, and Robert
Waller Rothwell, labourer and shop-keeper, had a
desultory discussion, at the close of which be-
tween thirty and forty names were given as the
nucleus of a society. It was agreed amongst them
to pay sixpence entrance, and twopence a week to
a common fund, to be increased by larger contri-
butions in case any of the members were thrown
out of work by the arbitrary conductof the masters
and thereby required relief. The agitators,
were apparently a small minority of the meeting,
and with no definite plan of action ; and as the
principal farmers hive given unasked 2s. Dd. per
day, besides allowing many important privileges
to got up an illnatured contention about the hours
of labour, which few farmers are strict to enforce ,
end threepenee a day underprosent eiretunstinee 8,
is considered a question3blo policy.

OLDHAM.
THE TRADES COUNCIL.

The usual quarterly meeting of the Oldham
Amalgamated Trades Council was held at the
Bath Hotel, on Tuesday evening, March 12th,
representatives of the following trades being pre-
sent :--Bricklayers, brass .finishers, cordwainers,
machine-grinders, hatters, joiners (general union),
old smiths, painters, skip-makers, tailors, spindle
and fly makers, joiners (amalgamated), tin-plate
workers, spinners and minders' association (eight
branches), printers, and plumbers. After some
local business had been transacted, a resolution
was passed, pledging the council not to rest satis-
fied until the disgraceful "Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act" was totally repealed. Resolutions
were also carried in favour of supporting the
"Mines' Regulation Bill," the " Master and Ser-
vant (Wages) Act," the "Workmen and Servants
Compensation Act," and the Bill Mr. Mundella
proposes to bring into the House of Commons
after Easter for the shortening of the:hours of labour
in factories for women and children.

articles.title: TUE IRON TRADE.
articles.text:
TUE IRON TRADE.

A combined meeting of the masters and work-
men of the Oldham iron trade was held on Monday
to discuss the question of payment for overtime,
and avert the threatened strike of 10,000 men.
The masters' proposed to pay time and an eighth
for the first four hours, leaving the subsequent
overtime for special arrangements. The men de-
manded time and a quarter the first two hours,
time and a half the second two hours, aud double
time afterwards. This and other minor idetnands
were conceded.

articles.title: MANCHESTER.
articles.text:
MANCHESTER.

TILE AMALGAMATED CARPENTERS' SOCIETY.

The following is from the March monthly
report :

FELLOW MEMBERS,—During the past month
the state of trade has gradually improved, the
number of members in receipt of donation benefit
being 113 less than it was a month ago. The
total number of members in the Society now
exceeds 10,000.

We have received no returns this month from
the Cardiff, Exmouth, Guildford, Hoxton, Lincoln,
Llangollen, Longton, Plymouth 2nd, Tunbridge
Wells, Wood Green, and Cork Branches.

The members of the Ilkley Branch, lleing
unable to secure the adoption of the nine hours'
system, have left the town, and the Branch has
been closed; the box, books, and funds being
forwarded to the general Oka—Signed on behalf
of the Council,

JOHN THOMPSON, Chairman.
JOHN D. Pinion, Gen. Sec.
Manchester, March Bth, 1872.

GLASGOW.
THE GREAT STRIKE AT LEEDS.

On Wednesday night, a deputation from the
Leeds flax spinners waited upon the Glasgow
Trades' Council, and after presenting their case,
asked the aid of the council, to enable them to
secure the end for which they have come out on
strike.

After consideration, the council agreed to issue
letters to the secretaries of the various societies of
factory operatives in Glasgow and neighbourhood,
recommending them to give the flax spinners of
Leeds pecuniary assistance during the struggle.
Assistance was granted to the men on strike in
Leeds, on Wednesday, to the amount of £270.

articles.title: YORK.
articles.text:
YORK.

THE CABINET MAKERS AND THE NINE HOURS.

A month ago an agitation was begun amongst
the cabinet makers of this ancient city, to secure
the 51 hours limit, in lieu of the 58? j, hours they
were then working. A meeting was called, a
committee was appointed, and a circular was
addressed to the various employers, asking for 54
hours to constitute a week's work, and that the
hours of working should be so arranged, as to
leave the workmen the enjoyment of the Saturday'
half-holiday. An answer was requested to be
sent, so as to be laid before a meeting of the men
on the 9th inst. On the 6th, however, a collective
answer from the masters 14' LIS received, to the
effect that they would grant the nine hours asked
for, but they should require the hours to be

different from those proposed by the men. The
masters proposed that work should begin at break-
fast time on Monday morning, and that four
o'clock (the present time) should be the closing
time on Saturday. A meeting of the men as
called for the same night, and these terms were
discussed. Whilst thankful the masters had con-
ceded the time asked for, the men declared the
boon to be almost neutralized by the arrangement
of the hours. A reply was accordingly sent,
asking for the half-day as first proposed, and
a meeting was arranged for the following Saturday,
the 9th, to receive the employers' reply.
In that reply, the masters stated they should ad-
here to the hours of work proposed in their first
letter to the men. At this intimation, the meeting
began to consider the advisability of some means
being adopted to induce the employers to reconsider
their decision, when it was stated that the men
working at two firms in the city (Messrs. Taylor
Brothers and Mr. Baynes), without consulting or
considering their fellow workmen, had mado their
own terms with their employers, and had agreed
to work till four o'clock OR Saturdays. At this
sign of disunion no resolution was come to ; but
on the following Monday----last Monday—the
men in many of the shops did not start work as
usual, but waited upon their several employers to
endeavour to secure better terms than those offered.
In most instances they were not successful, though
one master, Mr. Isaac Brown, has agreed to pay
his men for two hours' overtime on Saturday after-
noons, the exigencies of his business not allowing
him to give them the half day. The consequence
of the vacilating conduct of some of the men is,
that we, who would prefer to enjoy a half huh-

day on the day when nearly every other trade
is enjoying it, are condemned to the dingy se-
clusion of the workshop. It is to be hoped that
the men will not cease to agitate for the
half-day holiday till they get it, and that
they will see the necessity of a thorough union
amongst themselves. Although it was resolved
at the meeting, when the circular to the masters
was discussed, not to introduce the question of
wages, yet for many reasons it is a question that
must soon be brought forward. The average
wage-24 shillings per week—is so far behind
that of other trades, in which no more skill ia
required, that for the honour of the craft, and
the comfort of their families, the men are justified
in asking for an advance. What sound reason
can there be in a joiner receiving 28 shillings a
week, and a cabinet maker only 24 shillings ?
There is some talk of a society being formed ;
can only hope that it will succeed in bettering
6ur condition; but to do that it must have the
support of the whole of the men.

SALFORD.
THREATENED STRIKE OF RAILWAY ENGINEMEN

AND FIItEMEN.

On Sunday afternoon a well-attended meeting of
firemen, engine-guards, and guards, in the service
of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Com-
pany, was held at the house of Mr. Clowes,
"British Fleet," Oldfiold-road, Salford. There were
delegates present from Bury, Wigan, Miles
Platting, Wakefield, Bolton, Blackburn, Accring-
ton, and other stations on the Lancashire and
Yorkshire and East Lancashire systems, and several
representatives from the London and North-
Western Company's. The meeting had been con-
vened for the purpose of considering what steps
should he taken to enforce the general demand for
a reduction of the hours of work from twelve nod
a half to ten per day, for an increase of wages, and
for the remedying of various existing grievance*
as set forth in the memorial adopted at the meet-
ing recently held in the Free Trade Hall.
The Chairman and several delegates complained
that they had been "most uncourteously, and
abominably, and tyrannically treated!' by the
superintendent of the East Lancashire sectioo
since presenting the memorial; that he bad
plainly threatened to make matters worse for these
if they expressed further dissatisfaction; and that,
therefore, they were determined to a man—from
the youngest to the oldest, "to the very collar
buttons of their coats," to fight for their just
rights, as conceded by the directors in their agree-
ment of 1867, which had since been violated-0
take no further notice of their superintendents, but.
to wait, by deputation, upon Mr. Lawn, and if he
refused them justice to take measures which would.
compel them to grant their requests to the letter.
(Applause.)
A memorial, signed by 600 men, was unani-
mously adopted, and a deputation, consisting of
about twenty delegates, was appointed to wait
upon Mr. Lawn, and present it, together with a
letter of complaint against Mr. Hurst,superintendent
of the Lancashire and Yorkshire section, and Mr.
Jaques, superintendent of the East La ncashirs
section.

ANOTHER CASE OF INTIMIDATIov.

On Tuesday, at the Salford Town Hall, Jame.
M,:n-y was charged with intimidating workmen
employed at the Pendleton Ironworks. On Mon-
day evening the prisoner who is employed at tho
works, left off work about half-past five o'clock,
and returned again about seven in a state of semi
-
intoxication. He used very abusive language, ana
called the men " knobsticks." He got hold Of one
by the coat, and pushed him backwards into a
wheelbarrow, which was full of hot cinders. He
threatened another man, and said ho would throw
him into the furnace in which the iron was melted.
In consequence of the violent language and menace°
of the prisoner, two men put on their coats and
left their work. They said they were afraid of
their lives, and they could not be induced by the
manager to remain. Sir J. 1. Manton summa'
committed the prisoner for two months.

articles.title: MISCELLANEOUS TRADES.
articles.text:
MISCELLANEOUS TRADES.

At a largo meeting, held on Monday evening,
in the Town Hall, Hanley, it was decided to solicit
an addition of 6d. per day to the wages (4s. 6(1.)
now paid to firemen, dippers, placers, kilnraen,
and saggar makers.
An amicable arrangement of the dispute in the
Birmingham chain trade has been made, and the
yardmen will commence work on Monday next, id
the altered prices.
All the Pifeshiro minors will receive from the
20th inst. a uniform rise of 6d. per day of eight
,hours.
The floorcloth operatives of Kirkcaldy are of-
fered 51 hours weekly, but demand 51, and a
strike Ia considered imminent.

The operative boot and shoemakers of Sheffield
demand increased wages. _ _

The workmen of the Staffordshire potteries have
resolved on demanding an increase of 6d. per day
on the present rate, 45. 6d.

The carpenters and joiners of North Stafford-
shire are agitating for the nine hours.
The employs at Mr. Fosters, printer, Bear-
alley, Farringdon-street, havingp resented the Com-
positors' Memorial in February, waited upon him
for his answer. They met with a good reception,
that gentleman acceding to the terms of the me-
morial in its entirety. The movement commenced
on March Ist. It is hardly necessary to add that
it gave great satisfaction to all in the establish-
ment from the promptness with which it was
accorded.

At Mahon recently the builders—some of them
unsolicited—granted the nine hours limit. The
men, however, have had another meeting, and
have issued resolutions fixing an increase of wages
to 30s. per week in summer and 275. in winter
(with 52 hours per week) ; and these have been
sent to all employers "by order of the com-
mittee."

The master coach builders of Harrogate,
Messrs. Wright and Sens, and Mr. Beazley,
being solicited by their workmen for a reduction
of their weekly term of labour to 54 hours per
week, very cordially granted the same, com-
mencing from March 4th.
The employes of the firm of Messrs. Diprose and
Bateman, 13 and 17 Portugal-street, Lincoln's-
inn-fields, presented a petition on Tuesday evening
to their employers, for a Teduction in the hours of
work in a week to fifty-four; which favour was
very kindly granted. The nine hours movement
Will therefore commence in that establishment on
the first of next month. At a " chapel " held
afterwards it was decided to invite Mr. Diprose to
a supper in commemoration of the event.

articles.title: IMPENDING STRIKE OF THE LONDON COMPOSITORS.
articles.text:
IMPENDING STRIKE OF THE
LONDON COMPOSITORS.

IMPORTANT MEETING OF MASTER,

PRINTERS.

A largo end influential meeting of the master
Printers of the metropolis was held yesterday at
the Freemasons' Tavern, to consider the steps
desirable to be taken in view of the threatened
strike of the compositors for an advance in wages
and a reduction in the hours of labour. Mr. Gal-
pin, of the firm of Cassell, Fetter, and Galpin,
Ludgate-hill, occupied the chair, and nearly all
the large establishments were represented. About
200 gentlemen wore present, including Messrs.
Cloves, Waterlow, Rivington, M'Corquodale,
Wyman, Burt, Virtue, Adlard, Judd, Edwards,
Pardon, Rider, Straker, Taylor, Bcc., arc.

Mr. C. Wyman read a long report from the
oommittee of master printers detailing the corres-
pondence that had taken place between the com-
mittee and the council of the compositors' trade
society, in relation to the memorial which had
been received by, the masters from the society.
The memorial of the men asked for a reduction of
the hours of labour, from sixty to fifty-four per
Week, an alteration in the hours and payment for
overtime, and an advance of a id. per 1,000 letters
Upon all descriptions of bookwork. The conference
had taken place between the committees of the mas-
ters and the men, which, indeed,ended in a counter-
Proposal emanating from the Masters' Committee.
The masters positively refused to concede any ad-
'Vance whatever of wages, but were willing to
Concede 57 hours per week, or would agree to ac-
cept 64 hours, providing the scale of payment to
the establishment hands was re-arranged. These
alternative proposals had been submitted to an
aggregate meeting of the men held at Exeter
flail, on the 6th inst., and by thorn rejected in toto.
That meeting passed a resolution, insisting on the
full terms of the memorial being conceded, with
the exception that newspaper and parliamentary
Work was to be excepted from any advance; and
a further resolution was passed, declaring that,
unless the terms of the memorial were conceded
by Saturday, March 16th, the men should give the
usual fortnight's notice to leave their employment.
The report concluded by complaining of the want
of candour and consideration on the part of the
men, and their allowing themselves to be subjected
to the influence and dictation of their committee.
The Chairman said the committee had purposely
refrained in their Report from recommending any
tut and dried action to the meeting, thinking it
beat to leave the whole question open for consider.,
atioo- The practical question before the meeting
was, "What course were .the master printers
prepared to adopt, in view of the threatened
Strike of their workmen. (near.) The strike
'would undoubtedly take place, to a greater or
lesser
extent, and how were they going to face it ?
Mr. James Waterlow said he thought the manner

of the men more objectionable than their demands.
Be thought those demands exorbitant, but he did
not think the employers were in a condition to
resist them. (Hear and dissent.) He would,
therefore, make a virtue of necessity, and move—
" That the terms of the London society of Com-
positors as adopted by the meeting hold at Exeter
Hall be accepted by this meeting." (Hear, and
cries of "No, no.")
Mr. Allard seconded the resolution.

Mr. C. Wyman said ho could not accept the re-
solution. He was prepared to make a concession
in the hours, say, to 57 per week, but he would not
consent to the advanoe in wages. (Hear.) He
was in favour of meeting the strike boldly, and
testing the loyalty of their workmen. (Hear.)
He did not believe the bulk of his men would
leave him at the dictation of a tyrannical trades'
union. (Hear.) He moved as an amendment—
" That the memorial of the compositors be referred
to the action of individual employers."
Mr. Lawrence seconded the resolution.

A. long discussion ensued, in which Messrs.
Clowes, Burt, McCorquodale, Taylor, Judd,
Speaight, Johnson, and others took part. Several
suggestions were made for a compromise, others
recommending full concession to the men, and
others supporting the amendment, as they could
fight the men better in detail than as a united
body.
Mr. Ogden regretted to see the tone of the
masters was so desponding; ho was against all
concession. Let the council of the society and
their taols do their worst. The society had no
funds to support a strike. Ho did not believe
that one-third of the men, who would be intimi-
dated into giving notice, would actually leave at
the end of the fortnight.
The Chairman said the master printers of
London, even at the present rate of wages, were
unable to compste for general work with the
provincial and Scotch houses.
Ile then took the vote, when the amendment of
Mr. Wyman was carried with six dissentients,
about one half of the meeting not • voting either
way.

The' proceedings closed with a vote of thanks to
the chairman.

articles.title: FREE BREAKFAST TABLE.
articles.text:
A FREE BREAKFAST TABLE.

Sir Tollemache Sinclair has given notice of
his intention to move in the House of Com-
mons, on an early day, the following resolu-
tion :

That, in the opinion of this House, the taxes on
tea, sugar, and coffee, which are supplied as neces -
Banes of life, even to paupers in workhouses, which
bring £6,800,000 to the revenue, but cost about
£8,000,000 to the consumer, which are a greater
burden on the lower middle class than the income
tax, and which press with undue and special
severity on the women and children of the
manual labour class, who according to M.
Thiers, are taxed higher than in France on about
a million of outdoor paupers, a million of domestic
servants, a million of widows, and several millions
of orphan children, who are not now and are
never likely to be represented in Parliament,
should be immediately repealed, and that the
deficiency in the revenue thereby caused, after
allowing for the increased produce of the taxes on
tobacco, spirits, and malt, from the removal of the
taxes on the breakfast table, and the surplus cf
income over expenditure of this year, should be
made up by raising the duty on wine, the bever-
age of the rich, as soon as the French treaty is a
an end, to the same rate as on spirits, the beveiage
of the poor and lower middle classes, in proportion
to alcoholic strength, the duty on cigars and
tobacco to the same rate as in some of the British
colonies, the license duty on vendors of spirits,
beer,: and wino to a uniform graduated scale,
based on the unit of the present highest rate, and
by readjusting the house tax, so as to include all
houses which, if in the metropolis, would be worth
the present limit of £2O.

The Rev. Henry Marehmont, described as
a clerk in holy orders, having engaged in
extensive building speculations in Kensington
Park, presented a petition in bankruptcy; but
as he was suffering from nervous exhaustion,
and unable to attend for examination, the
sitting was adjourned for three months.

In its report on M. Lefrane's Press Prose-
cution Bill. the Commission states that the
measure goes no further than the repression
of "instigation to violent and illegal enter-
prises which constitute crimes ;" and denies
that, either directly or indirectly, it confers
the privilege of inviolability on the existing
non-definitive form of Government, "to which
the country has only given a provisional
adhesion.' The csommittee considers that its
task is limitel to enacting penalties against
attacks on the rights and the authority of the
Assembly; and glances at contingencies in
view of which "our prudence as legislators
should compel us to give to the Bill a formula
sufficiently broad, so as equally to protect
both the present and the future. Clause 2is
struck out; the committee considering that it
would practically subject the
t Whole of France
o martial law.

articles.title: CHURCH AND STATE.
articles.text:
CHURCH AND STATE.

MEETING AT HULL.

On Tuesday evening, Mr. George Potter gave an
address in the Protestant Hall, Kingston-square,
Hull, under the auspices of the Hull Reform
Union, on "The Disestablishment of the English
Church." Alderman Dowsing presided, and there
was a large audience. The proceedings through-
out were somewhat disorderly, applause and
hissing being freely indulged in by both parties.
The Chairman briefly introduced the lecturer,
whom he believed to be as good and staunch a
Protestant as there was in the country.
Mr. Potter, who was received with loud applause,
then addressed the meeting.
The following resolution was moved by the Rev
James Sibree, seconded by Mr. J. M. Stuart, an 1
supported by the Rev. Mr. Elstul

"That, in the opinion of this meeting, religious
equality is essential to just government, and cannot
exist under a State Established Church; and that
this meeting therefore expresses it cordial approval
of the efforts of Mr. Miall and others, in seeking
to obtain the disestablishment of the English
Church, and requests the Borough Members to
support Mr. Miall's motion for a commission of
inquiry into the revenue of that Church."
The resolution was carried with a few dis-
sentients.

Votes of thanks were carried by acclamation to
Mr. Potter and the chairman, which brought the
proceedings to a olose.

MEETING ON REDISTRIBUTION OF

SEATS.

On Wednesday night Mr. George Potter, of
London, delivered his second lecture in the
Protestant-hall, before the members of the Hull
Reform Union; Mr. G. IC. King presided over
a numerous audience.

The Chairman said the subject of the lecture,
"The Redistribution of Seats," was almost a now
one, and therefore they 'required information
hence they had obtained the' services of Mr.
George Potter for the purpose of discussing the
important question. That it was an important
one there could be no doubt. They wore in pos-
session of statistics whirl clearly proved that
many groat anomalies existed with respect. to
voters. Ho had before him a paper published in
Chelsea, from which he saw that,they were going
to have the subject introduced into the House of
Commons by Sir Chas. Dilke (loud cheers). He
would just read one paragraph to show a sufficient
reason why this subject should be discussed "to
show the necessity of dealing with this question,-1
(said Sir C. Dilke) need only refer to the vote on
a clause putting an end to payment for canvassing
introduced by Sir IL A. Hoare upon this question.
Although only 96 votes were recorded against,
and 69 in favour of that measure, an examination
of the constituencies represented showed that in-
stead of losing by 27 votes, we gained by 100,000."
If there was no other example of the inequality of
reptesentation than this, it was sufficient to prove
that there was necessity for altering this state of
voting (loud applause).
Mr. Potter then gave a most intereqing aldre SS
upon the subject, which was full of faLts and
figures, showing the great anomalies exist'n; in
the present system of Parliamentary representa-
tion.

Mr. Blackburn moved, and Mr. Avery seconded,
,ho following resolution :

"That, in the opinion of this meeting, the time
has arrived when, in order to secure an equitaLle
representation of the people in the Commons
House of Parliament, an amendment in the present
unjust distribution of seats has become imperative,
and this meeting pledges itself to aid to the best of
its ability the furtherance of this object."
The motion was carried unanimously.
Mr. Whitehead thoved, Mr. 'Upton seconded,
and Mr. Knowles supported, a resolution warmly
thanking Mr. Potter for his admirable address.
Thanks were likewise voted to the chairman by
acclamation.

On Tuesday morning a collision occurred on
the East Lancashire section of the Lane ashire
and Yorkshire Railway, in the vicinity of New..
church Station. A passenger train leaving
Manchester for Baoup had entered a tunnel,
when it came in collision with the tail end of
a goods train of 19 or 20 waggons, which was
running towards Bump. The whole of the
passenger train was enveloped in the darkness
of the tunnel at the time of the accident. The
guard of the goods train whistled vigorously,
but this warning does not appear to have boon
heard on the passenger engine, the driver of
whioh, however, having his suspicions aroused
of the proximity of the goods train by the
large presence of steam in the tunnel did not
proceed at the usual speed. The injury
inflicted was not very extensive, consisting in
the smashing of the van and engine buffers,
the shaking of the goods guard and some of the
passengers in the forepart of the latter train,
and the blocking of the line—a single one
from Rawtenstall to Baoup—for two hours
Or 00.

articles.text:
THE AMERICAN ANSWER TO EARL
GRANyILLE'S NOTE.

! The Tribune of March 3 says:
The form of the reply to Earl Granville's note
was determined in the Cabinet meeting to-day,
and the document, which covers about five
pages of °Moist paper, was sent off this
evening. The members of the Cabinet are
unwilling to make public the contents of the
reply, but say it is entirely friendly in form
and spirit—as much so as Granville's—and
that it will leave with England the entire
responsibility of breaking up the treaty, if it
fails at all. It is understood that Mr. Fish's
letter takes the ground thatwe can't withdraw
any part of our case as presented; that we
still hold that the text of the Treaty and the
general feeling on the part of the American
Commissioners, and a majority,at least, of the
Senate, and Americans generally, give us the
right to present claims for consequential da
ranges; that we would have no righ -
indeed to have withheld them, since we
should thus have failed to allow the treaty to
settle all the causes of difference between the
two nations. At the same time there is
understood to be a broad hint that the United
States will not be very much surprised or
diappointed if the Geneva Conference deeides
that we have no just claim on England for
indirect damages which, after all, can't ba
estimated in cash. Besisles, it is held that the
Geneva Conference is the only tribunal that
can decide over what matters its jurisdiction
extends, and that we are willing to stand by
the award of that tribunal, and will expect
, England to do the same. The President and.
Cabinet are understood to feel hopeful that,
unless some new political excitement
arises in England between now and the
meeting of the Geneva Conferense, tho ques-
tions in dispute will be allowed to go there,
and that the treaty will be sustained. The
fact that no protest against our case was made
for so many weeks after it was in the hands
of the British Cabinet, and that the excite-
ment arose just as Parliament was meeting,
and subsided when the vote testing the
strength of parties had been taken, convinces
our Government that the whole proceedingt
was a political necessity on the part of the
Gladstone Ministry, and that it will be so,
anxious to find its way out of the tribaual
that it will be successful.

THE PUBLIC HEALTH BILL.
Mr. Stansfuld's Public Health Bill has been
printed. To those who insist upon consolida-
tion as necessary before all things, the ,hill

some extent.we share that feeling, but it is
impossible to ignore the force of the oonaider,
ations which led the Government to. eenfina
its attention for the present to, the work o4`

come in time; it is even possible thAt it may
be attempted • by Mr. Stansfeld this session.
But whether this proves to he the ease or not,
Parliament has before it the Bill of Sir Charles
AdderleY, and can decide the question for it-
self. The Ministerial Bill is largely devciked
to the creation of effective machinro for
working the existing and future Saiii4kry Acts,
Mr. Stansfeld has evidently bestowed groat
labour upon this part of his
,aohatne, and it is
but doing him the barest justice to. aeluito:-.
ledge that he has stiogeed.e4 in bringiag order
out of -confusion. It will no longer be donbt-
ful who is responsible for the executinn of tlw
, law. Autherkty has been consolidated, ii 44
, the permissive 'character of past legialation
has been largely modified. We could have
wished for a more stringent system of com-
pulsion, and we hope the Bill in its progress,
through Parliament will he amended here and,
