articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

Her Majesty, accompanied by Prince Leo-
pold and Princess Beatrice, arrived in London
from Windsor ou Monday afternoon.

It is stated that the Villa Cavendish, for-
merly occupied by NI. Etnilo do Girardin, at
Baden, has been taken for the Queen for six-
teen days from the 27th inst.

On Monday a deputation waited upon Lord
Northbrook urging the development of the
railway and canal communication in India,
the encouragement of experiments tending to
improve the cultivation of cotton, and the
granting of fair play to the submarine tele-
graph companies. his, lordship, while ad-
mitting the immense importance of the ques-
tion as it affected the cultivation of cotton,
reminded his hearers that some consideration
should be shown to the interests and even to
some extent the prejudices of the people of
India, The other subjects should receive his
best attention, and he would at all times be
glad to consider any suggestions or expressions
of opinion from those who were qualified to
offer them.

At the Mailborough-street Police-court on
Monday, Mr. Frederick Cox, honorary sec-
retary to the Free Dormitory Association,
again appeared on a summons charging him
with having obtained money by false pre-
tences. Amongst the witnesses were the Earl
of Carnarvon and Sir C. Trevelyan. The
hearing was again adjourned.

In tho French Assembly, on Monday, a
tumult occurred whioh is described as the
greatest that has ever occurred iu that body.
The subject under debate was the proposal of
a Committee to censure one of the members,
M. Pierre Lefrano, and prosecute another,
M. Itouvier, for some attacks which they had
made upon the Assembly in certain news-
papers. General Changarnier opposed the
proposal, and moved that the House should
pass to the order ot the day. This the
Committee accepted. Thereupon a member
of the Right cried out that though the Left
might regard the motion as an amnesty of
impunity, his party would regard it as one of
"disdain." It was this remark which occa-
sioned the tumult. For several minutes furious
exclamations were exchanged between Left
and Right, and when MM, Lofrano and
Ranvier addressed the House they were met
with persistent groans. M. Ales Fevre could
scarcely obtain a hearing owing to the uproar.
Ultimately the order of the day was passed,
notwithstanding violent protests from the
Left, which lasted for ten minutes after-
wards. During part of this *may sitting of
the French Assembly, the Prince of Wales
was present. He had previously paid a visit
to M. niers. His Royal Highness looked, it
is said, extremely well. '

Pius IX. held a reception on Sunday, and
made a speech, in which be said that the
misfortunes of the Church principally dated
from 1848, and that although it was impossible
for two Powers to exist side by side in Rome,
he hoped tranquillity would be re-established.
The report that preparations are making at
the Vatican for the departure of his Holiness
is once more denied.

A manifesto has been issued at Madrid in
the name of the Carlists, which states that the
Duke of Madrid advises all his adherents to
vote at the coming elections. Senor Sagasta
has issued a circular to the Governors of the
Provinces, urging them to respect the law in
the coming elections, and cause it to be re-
spected by the opposition.

The Joint Committee of both Houses of
Parliament to consider the railway, amalgama-
tion schemes now before the Legislature again
sat on Monday, When Mr. Al'port, general
manager of the Midland line, was examined
at some length. He was in favour of all the
railwaysin the kingdom being in the hands of
half a dozen amalgamated companies, which
should extend to each other running powers.
Mr. Grierson, manager of the Great Western,
was the only other witness, and the Committee
adjourned.

The doors of the " Hole-in-the-Wall "
Kirby-street, Hatton-garden, have been closed
against all assemblages of a democratic
character, in consequence of a complaint of
the noisy political meetings held in that
hostelry. The democrats have resolved to
form a 'Working Men's Club, by which means
they will be enabled to hold such gatherings
upon their own premises.

--
The Prince and Princess of Wales left
London on Saturday evening for the Conti-
nent. The Royal children remain at present at
Marlborough House.

Earl Stanhope presided at the annual
general meeting of the Royal Literary Fund,
and announced that the King of the Belgians
had consented to preside at the anniversary
festival on the Bth of May.

The Lord Mayor presided on Monday over a
meeting at the Mansion-house, to consider the
best means of providing funds for the com-
pletion of Bt. Paul's Cathedral. It was
pointed out by, more than one speaker that
the Thanksgiving for the recovery of the
Prince of Wales would be incomplete without
some national thank-offering to mark the
people's gratitude, and that the most suitable
form for such thank-offering would be the
finishing of Wren's masterpiece. These
views were embodied in a resolution, which
was moved by Mr. Beresford Hope, M.P.,
while other resolutions invited those present
to follow the example of the Queen, the Prince
of Wales, and the Duke of Edinburgh in
signing the subscription list, and requested
the co-operation of the country in an essen-
tially national work.

Mr. Stafford, Allen, a member of the Com-
mittee of the Anti-Slavery Society, is a can-
didate for the seat in the London School
Board, vacant through the resignation of Mr.
M'Cullegh Torrens, M.P.

Her" Majesty's approbation of the military
arrangements on the 27th ult., and of the ad-
mirable conduct of the troops, seamen, and
marines then on duty, has been conveyed in a
General Order by command of the Duke of
Cambridge.

The Comte de Chambord, instead of going
to Amsterdam, has left B.reda for Cologne.

The Princess Louise and the Marquis of
Lorne, who have been travelling in Germany
for some time, arrived in London on Saturday.

A Cabinet Council was held on Saturday,
which was attended by all the Ministers.

On Saturday the Master of the Rolls made
orders for winding up the Towns Drainage
and Sewage irtilisation Company and the
Tramway itailway. Company of Great
Britain.

In the French Assembly, on Saturday, the
question respecting M. Pouyer-Quertier's re-
signation was put to the Ministers by M.
Guiraud, and a very animated debate was the
result. M. Guiraud led the way by some dis-
cursive remarks, in which he attacked the
policy of M. Thiers, and caused much agita-
tion and tumult. M. Ponyor-Quertier then
addressed the House and contrasted the im-
poverished state of die treasury when he took
office with its present brilliant position. He
afterwards defended the course he had taken
with regard to M. Sanvier do la Motte, who he
believed had never misappropriated a sou of
public money. M. Casimir Perier and M.
Flufaure spoke on behalf of the Government,
and M. Gambetta, having defended himself
from a charge which he considered had been
brought against him by M. Pouyer-Quertier,
of having misappropriated public money, the
order of the day was adopted.

From an official statement which has been
made to M. de Remusat, the French Minister
for Foreign Affairs, it appears that all the
French soldiers imprisoned. in Germany have
been pardoned by the Emperor, except those
who had committed fresh offences after being
sentenced.

According to the Paris Constitutionnel, the
French Government has asked the Italian
Government for explanations respecting some
fortifications on the Genoese coast 'which are
supposed to be directed against Nice and
Savoy.

The Colon°loy of tho 50th (Queen's Own)
Regiment of Foot is vacant by the death, on
the 7th instant, of Lieutenant-General Marcus
John Slade.

A meeting of metropolitin commanding
°fliers was held on Saturday, when the report
of a Committee, lately appointed to make
inquiries respecting the arrangements for the
forthcoming Volunteer field-day at Brighton
and Lewes, was adopted. A resolution was
then moved by Colonel Du Plat Taylor,
pointing out the necessity of the strictest
discipline, and requesting commanding officers
to enforce amongst their men the duty of
conducting themselves as• good soldiers on
Easter Monday, This was carried. by a
majority of 12 to 5 over an amendment, sub-
mitting that the Volunteers should be subjeot
to military order and. discipline from their
departure until their return.

A numerously, attended meeting, held at
Oxford on Saturday, pledged itself to continue
the work begun by
.the late Bishop Patteson,
and 'called upon the Legislature to take
measures for suppressing the slave trade in
the Pacific.

Mr. J. Reginald Yorke, who sat in tho last
Parliament for the borough of Tewkesbury,
was on Monday returned without opposition
for East Oloucestershire, where a vacancy
had arisen in consequence of the resignation of
Mr. R. S. Holford, one of the Conservative
members for that division.

According to a report in Brussels, all the
Powers having commercial treaties with France
have declined to enter into any arrangements
with a view to the modification of those
treaties.

A banquet to Lord Northbrook, on his
appointment to the Governor-Generalship of
India, was given by the Mayor of Winchester
on Saturday evening. Elis lordship, in
response to the toast of his health, paid a
warm tribute to the memory of the late Lord
Mayo, and in briefly glancing at the principles
winch should govern the policy of Indian
administration, took his stand upon her
Majesty's proclamation of 18.58, on the transfer
of the Government from the East India
Company to the Crowd: lie had served for
some years in the India-office, and had at all
events learnt one great lesson, viz, the
difference between East and West, and
between eastern and western civilization, and
the danger of being carried away by ideas of
what may be right, politic, and wise in this
country when one was brought to deal with a
country and people of different sentiments,
religion, education, and tone of thought. Mr.
Grant Duff, M.P., Under-Secretary for India,
was amongst the other speakers.

The election at Wallingford, on Saturday,
when Mr. E. Wells was returned without
opposition in the room of the into Mr. Stanley
Vickers, is the eighth which has taken place
since the opening of Parliament. The net
result is the return of four Conservatives, two
Liberals, and two advocates of Home Rule for
Ireland; viz., Mr. P. S. Powell, for the North-
west Riding; Major W. F. Tollemache, for
West Cheshire; the Hon. G. E. Milnes
Monekton, for North Notts; Mr. Wells, for
Wallingford; Lord Richard Grosvenor, for
Flinthhire ; Mr. Pendery, for the Wick Burghs;
Captain Nolan, for Galway; and Mr. Blenner-
hassett, for Kerry.

The Brighton Daily News • says :—" Infor-
mation has been furnished to us that the
Church Association has, in the suit of Heb-
bed v. Purchas, acted on the writ of seques-
tration of the Rev. J. Purehas's goods by
employing four bailiffs to Bien the rev, gentle-
man's property. The officers were, we are
informed, instructed to examine every ward-
robe and chest of drawers in the .house—ex-
cept those containing the property of the ser-
vants—as well as the private drawers in the
library. Mr. Parehas's property is protected
by a deed of -gift, but special warrant has, it
is stated, been applied for to seize and sell the
wearing apparel of Mrs. Purohas and family,
and also the rev, gentleman's clothes." The
Brighton paper goes on to say on authority
that it is not true, as has been reported, that
the above proceedings are taken because a
compromise submitted to the incumbent of
St. James's has been rejected by that gentle-
man. The terms of a compromise were being
considered by Mr. Purehas when the officers
entered his residence.

A case of considerable mercantile interest
was decided by Viee-Chancellor Moline. Mr.
Joseph Wilson, a Liverpool merchant, in ob-
taining advanees from the Union Bank of
Liverpool on security of the Kenilworth, then
outward bound to Calcutta, added by way of
collateral security the interest held by his
mother in another ship called the Refuge.
The mortgage was registered May 18th, but
on the 12th Mrs. Wilson had taken from her
son an instrument securing to her whatever
should be earned by the Kenilworth on the
homeward voyage. Joseph Wilson failed a
month after the security was given, and there
was a race between his agent and that of' the
bank, to gain possession of the homeward-
bound ship. The bank agent sucoeeded in
boarding her before she arrived in port at
Marseilles, and the Vice-Chancellor ruled that
the bank must be held to be mortgagees of the
ship, and entitled to all her freight, and con-
sequently the bill of Mrs. Wilson, who was
much to be compassionated, must be dismissed
with costs.

Monday's storm in the French Assembly
has been followed by an after-swell even more
formidable than the original perturbation.
Deputy Sehoeleher accused M. Vitet, the
interim. President, of having grossly violated
the rules of tho House. Amid extreme
agitation provoked by this speech, M. Vitet
—who was not in the chair—defended his
conduct, and demanded the suppression of
words employed by M. Brisson, to the effect
"that if the President allowed the Official
Journal to say that a vote had been taken,
the report would be false." M. Brisson de-
clined to withdraw, the words, and accused
M. Vitet of three distinct breaches of the
rules. The uproar soon became extreme;
the Deputies left their seats with violent
gesticulations and cries; and finally the
interim President for the day, M. St. Marc
Girardin—like Herr Bookum-Dolff on an
historic occasion—put on his hat and sus-
pended the sitting: After a pause of nearly
half an hour, business was resumed, and as
M. Brisson stuck to his words, an ordinary
vote of censure was passed upon him by a
great majority.

After two years, the Manhunt divorce case
again crops up to the surface. Convinced that
his wife is hopelessly insane, Sir Charles Nor-
daunt sought to have his petition dismissed in
the Divorce Court, so as to allow him to appeal
to the House of Lords. Lord Penzance saw no
reason why he should not do so, and the
original petition was accordingly dismissed..

Owing to the promotion of a Tramway
Company at Sheffield, the Sheffield Carriage
Company (Limited) have agreed to sell the
goodwill of the omnibus routes along Whiell
the tramways are to run, and also the horses
and omnibuses at present in use thereon.
This course has been adopted in order to
prevent rivalry of an unprofitable nature.

The Mayor of Portsmouth's de!jeuner• to
Lord Northbrook has been fixed for MoudtlY
next.

The Committee presided over by Mine.
Thiers haft now in course of construction sixty -
nine cottages in the departments of the
Ardennes, Loiret, Seine-et-Oise, Meurthe-et-
Moselle, Seine, Eure-et-Loire, and Cote-d'Ors
and others will shortly be commenced.

Mgr. Guibert, Archbishop of Paris, 1115
caused two tablets in black marble to be
placed on the transept of Notre Dame, on one
of which are inscribed the names of the eccle-
siastical hostages, and on the other those of the
gendarmes, serjents.de-ville, and laymen
murdered by the Commune.

• A Times telegram says it seems certain
that the negotiations with the German
Government for the anticipatory evacuation
of French territory had been entered upon
before the retirement of M. Pouyer-Quertier.
These negotiations have for basis the pay-
ment of the three milliards between the
31st of December next and the 31st of
December, 1876, one milliard to be paid in
the current year, and one milliard and a
half in each of the four following years.

Mr. J. Walter, M.P., has presented the
Rev. George A. M. How, Vicar of St.
Gabriel's, Bromlev, to the Vicarage of Brom-
ley St. Leonard, -Middlesex, vacant by the
preferment of the Rev. Augustus George How,
B.D. to the Rectory of Doynton near
Bath'.

The Rectory of St. Mary's Afanchester has
become vacant by the death of the Iv. E. A.
Lang, M.A. It is worth £2OO a year, awl
is in the gift of the Dean and Canons of
Manchester.

The Dean and Canons of Bristol have pre-
sented the Rev. Edward Girdlestone, M.A.,
vicar of Halberton, near Tiverton, to the
Vicarage of Olverston, near Bristol, vacant by
the death of the Rev. Canon Mosely. The
Vicarage of Halberton, which became vacant
by Canon Girdlestone's preferment, is in the
gift of the Dean and Chapter of Bristol. The
Bishop of Hereford has instituted the Rev. W.
P. Stanhope, M.A., curate of Horn Lacy, to the
Vicarage of that parish, on the nomination of
Sir E. F. Stanhope, Bart.

Lord Eustaee Cecil the other day, asked the
Chairman of the Metropolitan Board of Works
whether, considering that Leicester-square has
now been for some years under the control Of
the Metropolitan Board of Works, the Board
has as yet come to any decision upon the best
manner of laying out the ground; and, if not,
what prospect there is, within a reasonabie
time of the railings outside being repaired, all
of the plot of ground inside being put in order.

Mr. Cowper-Templo will move the rejection
of the Epping Forest Bill, on the motion for
the second reading. The rejection of the
Commons Protection Bill is to be moved 11
Mr. Gregory.

Captain his Royal Highness the Duke of
Edinburgh, R.N., was entertained at dinner
on Tuesday evening by Colonel Barnard awl.
the officers of the Royal Marine ArtillerY,
the head-quarters of the corps, Eastney, no"
Portsmouth.

Prince Sootchai Bhanuwongse, a gentleman
of colour' is now pursuing his studies at
Balliol College, Oxford. The young E
is remarkably handsome, dresses and lives in
the best possible style, and is said to eniq
undergraduate life thoroughly. astern.

A. police-constable; who was attached to the
X division, was charged at Wandsworth with
having stolen a quantity of property belogin,i
to a Mr. Hole, of Brighton, with whose
the prisoner had eloped. He was cominittea
for trial.

A letter has been Rublished in. Paris by 61°
of the delegates from Metz who attended the
Commission appointed to inquire into the con-
duct of Marshal Bazaine in surrendering that
place. The delegates consider that the mar-
shal acted in a highly criminal manner, and
say that his punishment will be a satisfaction
to outraged public morality.

MARCH 16, 1872.

At the Westminster Police Court on Tues-
day a betting min was fined £5 for having
created an obstruction in Knightsbridge, and
£4 10s. for an assault upon two constables
who arrested him.

Mr. W. H. Bullock, who acted as the Coal-
pussioner of the French Peasant Relief Fund,
instituted by the Daily News during the war
between France and Germany, has been ap-
pointed Chevalier of the Legion of Honour by
the French Government.

Mr. Disraeli, desiring to make only one
address, the city of Manchester, as the most
central point, has been fixed upon as the place
of assembly.

It is announced from Calcutta that several
deaths from cholera occurred among the
troops of the Looshai Expedition.

False rumours of a Bonapartist plot having
been discovered, and several arrests made,
have circulated in Paris. Apropos of the con-
spiracy in which Mazzini was said to have
been engaged at the time, we hear from Berne
that a detective officer has been sent by the
Federal Council to the Canton Ticino, "to
watch the Italian revolutionary proceedings
which are being secretly carried on there.'

Senor Ortega by Royal decree of King
Amadeus, has been authorised to lay a sub-
marine cable between a point on the English
coast and the mouth of the Bidassoa,.near
Trun, in Spain, to be ready in two years.

"Erie," it would seem, is no longer to re-
main a name of reproach to American finance
and of sorrowful meaning to English share-
holders. The directorate of the railway has
been remodelled, after a stiff fight against the
Gould party, who were finally compelled to
give way. General Dix has been chosen
President, General McClellan superintendent,
and other gentlemen of credit and position
take seats at the Board. The issue of the
elections has given unqualified satisfaction to
all but Mr. Jay-Gould and his adherents, who
threaten to cOntest the result in a court of
justice—a threat which, it may be hoped,
will lead to no disturbance of a Board "known
to be in favour of mike justice to the English
shareholders."

Her Majesty -held a Drawing Room at
Buckingham Palace on Tuesday afternoon,

A powerful gathering of the Orleanist
family took place at the Hotel Bristol in. Paris
on Tuesday, when the Prince and Princess of
Wales entertained at luncheon the Prince
and Princess de Joinville, the . Duo
d'Aumale,_the Comte and Comtesse de Paris,
and the Duo de Nemolug. In the afternoon
M. Thiers came to the had topay his respects,
and afterwards their Royal Highnesses drove
out unattended—the Prince seeming in excel-
lent health. •

Ragpielcing is not often so productive as it
proved to Margaret Welsh, who it was stated,
found a purse containing over £3O, hidden by
the wife of a marine store dealer in a rag-bin.
She was tempted to exclaim, "What. good
rags these are ! " She was accused at Marl-
borough-street of appropriating the purse, and
remanded without bail.

A page-boy was charged at Clerkenwell
with having attempted to poison his master,
the Rev. C. Reade of Islington, by putting
antimony in a bottle of brandy. It was
alleged that the lad wail incensed at being
dismissed from his situation. Mr. Cooke
said it was a very serious charge, and remanded
the prisoner.

Association has been favoured with the
following official communication: "Post-
office, Ipswich, March 2.—Sir,—When pass-
ing along the road from Ipswich to Wood-
bridge to-day I observed notices of a meeting
of Republicans, &0., posted on two of the
posts for the new line of telegraph. No nam e
Was attached to these notices, but, as chairman,
You are responsible for the aots of your
'°ointY. The penalty for defacing Government
property varies from 403. fine to two year's
121Prillonment. I therefore give you notice
iliq.unlesa these bills are at once removed I
n_Pail apply for a summons against you.—l am,
y2yonr, °bottle* nt servant, J. RA.MSEY, Lieut.
-ME, Government Superintendent of Tele-
graphs. To the Chairman of the Ipswich
Republicans."

The bill brought in by Mr. Lowe and Mr.
Baxter relating to the land reclaimed from the
Thames Embankment has been printed. It
authorises the Metropolitan Board of Works
to acquire the land in question for the sum of
£40,000, or such a sum as may bo settled by
two arbitrators, one appointed by the Govern,
%eat and the other by the Board of Works, or
by an umpire lathe event of the arbitrators dis-
Illtreeing. The Board is to have power to
borrow the money- to pay for the land, or they
ratty, if they think fit, elect to pay it by a per-
petual rent-charge or annuity.

Within a very short time after the decease
of the Rev. john
.Foreman, whose public
funeral at Kensal-green has already been
noticed, the Strict Baptist Calvinistic Church
has lost another Of its foremost ministers in
the metropolis, in the person of the Rev. James
Wells, who• died at his residence in Lough
borough Park, on Sunday last, at the age of
69. The sphere of Mr. Wells's labours was
the Surrey Tabernacle, Wansey-street, Wal-
worth-road, a handsome edifice built by his
congregation seven years ago, at a cost of
£12,000. He had been 42 years in the ministry,
but had recently suffered from ill-health, not
having preached since November, 1870.
His congregation it saidto have beentlie largest
one of Strict Baptists in existence, numbering
about 2,000. Mr. Wells was entirely a self-
educated man, and possessed of extraordinary
ability and energy.

The 'Gazette announces that " the Queen
has been pleased to direct letters patent to be
passed under the Great Seal, granting the
dignity of a Baronet of the United Kingdom
of Great Britain and Ireland unto the Right
Honourable Sills John Gibbons, of Sitting-
bourne, in the county of Kent, Lord Mayor of
the City of London, and the heirs male of his
body lawfully begotten." The Queen has ap -
pointed Colonel John Cox Gawler to be
Keeper of the Jewels in the Tower of London,
in the room of Colonel Charles Wyndham,
deceased.

The Consul-General of the Unitod States
informs us that reports have now reached him
of the contributions for the relief of Chicago
raised in each consular district of the United
Kingdom. The total of these subscriptions is
£162,363 us.

Mr. William Rathbone, M.P., who has
been moving in the matter of improved
telegraphic communication between Liverpool
and London, has sent a communication to
Mr. Blood, secretary to the Liverpool Chamber
of Commerce, to the effect that when the
telegraph service is removed to the new
buildings, Mr. Scudaraore intends to establish
a direct wire between the Commercial Sale-
rooms in Mincing Lane and the Liverpool
Exehange Rooms, and that he hopes to be able
to grant the same facility to the Liverpool
Corn Exchange.

Preparations are being made for holding
national exhibition at Madrid in 1873. Space
will be allotted to foreign exhibitors.

News from the Cape of Good Hope states
that Sir Henry Barkly has been appointed
Governor of West Griqualand, which is the
official name for the diamond-fields. Dia-
monds wore still being sold by auction, but
prices had declined. It is mentioned that
spurious diamonds had been imported into the
colorry from Birmingham. From the gold-
fields favourable accounts have been received.

A S. Paul (Minnesota) despatch states
that Mr. M`Nab's North Shore Railway sur-
veying party, consisting of twenty-five men,
is believed to have perished in a storm on the
lake, some distance off the west end of Isle
Royale; on the 24th of January.

The difference between the Birmingham
Town Council and. the School Board of that
borough has been adjusted by the latter
body undertaking that no part of the £4,000
required for educational purposes should be
applied to payments in aid of denominational
schools during the present year. 011 this
understanding the council have granted the
money.

Murphy, the well-known anti-Popery
leoturer, died on Tuesday evening at Spark-
brook, Birmingham.

A telegram has been received from Mel-
bourne announcing that the native village
in the island where Bishop Patteson was
murdered has been shelled and, destroyed by
her Majesty's sloop Rosario.

The Government of Versailles has awarded
to Mr. Gordon Leslie, of Alton, Hants, the
Ribbon and Cross of Merit, together with its
Special Diploma, as "a token of gratitude for
devoted services in behalf of the sick and
wounded." Mr. Leslie's comrade, Mr. Harri-
son, also from Alton, never recovered from the
fatigues and exhauStion he had undergone,
and died at Madeira, where ho had gone for
his health.

Mr. Spencer Ponsonby, Comptroller of the
Lord Chamberlain's Department, is gazetted a
C.D., and Lord Poltimere has been appointed
Treasurer of the Household, in the room of
Lord do Tabby, resigned.

Resolutions were passed by a numerous
meeting of Suez Canal Company shareholders,
In Paris, approving the action of the directorate
in suppressing the journal of the company, in
organising a new system of collecting dues,
and in refusing to convert the existing inter.
national association into a Fren.oh joint-stook
company.

Two hundred and ninety-four patients
were relieved at tho Hospital for Diseases of
the Skin during the week ending March 9th.

The Duo d'Aumale was nominated a General
of Division on Sunday, and received' the
ordinary communication from the Minister of
War. The Committee on Primary Instruc-
tion has informed M. Jules Simon that it
rejects the text of the bill, M. Jules Simon
said he would defend in the Assembly the
existence of a moral system independent of
the Gospel.

The Marquis of 4neensberry has been elec-
ted one of the Scotch Representative Peers,
in the room of the Earl of Katie, deceased.

So many unauthorised and distressing
statements have been circulated concerning
the hopeless condition of Lady Charles lanes
Ker, that we are glad to be able to state that
many of the worst symptoms are passing
away, and that the healing processes of re-
pair and absorption are obviously in progress.

The Deputy Recorder of the City, Mr. T.
Chambers, M.P. for Marylebone, is to• be
knighted. The same honour is also to be
awarded to Mr. Goss, the organist of St.
Paul's, who officiated at the Thanksgiving
Service; and to Mr. John Coode, C.E., who
has for twenty-five years superintended the
Portland Breakwater just completed.

A deputation of brewers waited the other
day upon the Chancellor of the Exchequer, to
urge upon him, as a matter of justice, the
repeal of the brewers' licence duty, in place
of which they would not objeot to a duty of
is. per quarter on malt. Mr. Lowe promised
to consider their case.

Stinday was the ninth anniversary of the
marriage of the Prince and Princess of Wales,
which was celebrated March 10th, 1863.

Prince Arthur patronised a concert on
Thursday, given at Dover by Madame Couneau,
wife of the physician of Napoleon, and who is
compelled to turn her musical gifts to a profit-
able account.

The Duke of Edinburgh has consented to be
patron of the Society Missions to Seamen,
and has sent £2O in aid of its funds.

Of the Looshai Expedition, General Bour-
chicereports, in a despatch dated the sth inst.,
that the forces under his command have com-
menced their return home. A portion of the
force bad already left for Cachar, The Looshai
tribes were behaving in a friendly manner.

The Prince of Wales's Thanksgiving was
observed at Dresden by avelebratiou of the
Holy Communion at 8 a.m. and Mathis (choral)
at 11 a.m. in All Saints' Church. It was a
day of sincere rejoicing.

The Duchess de Persigny, who had returned
to France to attend the funeral of her husband,
has left for Egypt, where she had left her
youngest daughter in delicate health.

A telegram says that the Archbishop of
Posen has not only been appointed, hut has
already acted as Primate of all Poland, advis-
ing the Pope on the recent Episcopal appoint-
ments for the Russian territory.

The Dublin University Boat Club has
resolved to send a crew to Henley Regitta.

Admiral Sir John Soott, K.C.8., died at
Cheltenham on the 2nd inst., aged eighty-one.
He had three medals for services in the wars
with France, China, and the United States.

blTallog, were tried for the murder of Ann,
wife of Owen biTadden, and sister-in-law to
a brother of the accused. There was an
agrarian feud between the parties, and

The revision of the Swiss constitution being
now completed, the vote of the people upon
the changes made is to be taken on the 12th
of May.

gate-street station of the Metropolitan Rail-
way, an assault upon a passenger was com-
mitted by a porter, for which a fine of 40s.
was on Wednesday inflicted at the Guidliall
Police-court. Alderman liesley, in giving
his decision, took occasion to say that the
officials at Aldersgate•street were "not so
civil as they might be."

had long infested the neighbourhood of Cor-
dova, has just been shot by the gendarmes of
that town.

India and Pacific Company's steamer Colum-
bia foundered at the island of St. Thomas.
We now learn that she has been raised, and
that tile damage she has sustained is so slight
that it can be repaired for a few thousand
dollars. It is stated that the addresses on the
cargo are still legible.

Baker-street carriage bazaar on Wednesday
were some State carriages of the ex-Emperor
Napoleon, but the prices realised were far
below the original cost. The equipages were
purchased by an undertaker, who is about to
convert them into mourning coaches,

relief. Compared. with the corresponding
weeks in 1871, 1870, and 1869, this was a

man, was on Wednesday released from Rich-

WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE
rROMOTING TUE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO TILE WORKING CLASSES OV GREAT BRITAIN.

FELLOW WORKMEN,—
The Working Men's Committee has been formed
in consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and State must be referred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last' Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Miall to
the judgment of the House of' Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation of immediate
success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Irelend,he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature to
apply the principle of that measure to the rest of
the United Kingdom. He was met with ,the objee-
tion that the case of Ireland was peculiar—which
indeed it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendewmtnt and disestablishnu nt
of the State-Church in Ireland, did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the quOstion was not yet ripe for legislative action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Miall, that he must first convince a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.
This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
been accepted ; and the Society for the Liberation
of Religion from State-Patronage and Control has
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. . The Working Men
of Great Britain have never yet, as a body, pro.
flounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has been felt that, after the broad challenge thrown
down by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either.to him or to themselves, refrain from
a declaration of their hottest and deliberate senti-
ments. From Mr. Miall, and the great party that
he has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
leader of the Liberal party in the House of Com-
mons, and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Men, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not.simply Upoll the purely numerical
ground suggested by Mr. Gladstone, as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour of, or against, the Dis-
endowment and Disestablishment of the State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland; but also,
and perhaps especially, with a view to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General. Election, whensoever that may take
place. The House of Commons, as now consti-
tuted, does not embody a faithful and com-
plete representation of the whole people; and,
without taking a poll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the challenge of the Pre-
mier consists in the election of a House of Commons,
, each member of which has been returned with a
special view to his avowed opinion on the great
question thus gravely put to the issue.

These then, are the circumstances under which
the Working Men's Committee for promoting the
Separation of Church and State has been formed,
and now proceeds to work.
The views of the Committee may be thus con-
sisely stated-
1. They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must be loft between man and his Maker.

2. They arc of opinion that, since the State
Church in one part of the United Kingdom has
been disesttblished, it is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the 'United
Kingdom
3. They arc persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church is utterly
failed to accoMplish the task for which it was
established; and are also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects which churches of any
kind profess to keep in view.
.

4. The State-Charob of England has failed as
manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk of the
Irish People wore Boman Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed Protestantism of the then
State-Church, tho great majority of the British
People arc either members of the different Pro-
testant Nonconformist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselves to the
,Establish-
ment.

6. The immense revenues of the English and
Scottish Establishments 'alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance; because
those revenues, though the common property
of the whole nation,- are distfibuted among the
religious teachers of half, or less than half, of thee
people. Enormous and disproportionate salaries
and emoluments are paid to Bishops and other
Dignitaries, while, of that portion of the fund
which is received by the parochial clergy, by far
the largest part falls to those who have the fewest
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations.
O. The obstructiveness of the Establishment is
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy are neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People. Jealous
of their own privileges, they resist all changes
which may affeet their own ascendancy, or that of
the Establishment in which they have so strong
vested interest. Hence, in every agitation of a
political or social character, they are always on
one side and the People on the other.
7. The Establishment is a source of national
-weakness, because it divides the nation into two
hostile parties. It prevents good men Uniting, as
they otherwise might unite, in works of philan-
thropy and in movements for social reform. It
thus Carries a mischievous sectarianism into almost
all the affairs of life..

Such aro the questions which the Committee of
Working Men commend to the serious consideration
of their fellow workmen throughout the Country.

In order to ascertain and give effect to their views,
Branch Committees will be formed, and meetings
held, in all thelar,,e towns. It is hoped, and believed,
that the practical result will be that, after this
great question has been submitted to the electors,
when it is next debated in the House of Commons,
Mr. Miall will be in a position to give to Mr.
Gladstone's challenge a satisfactory and decisive
answer.—We are, on behalf of the Wollaug
Men's Committce, Yours faithfully,
GEORGE HOWELL (Chairman).

SATURDAY, MARCH 16, 1872.

TfIE DEATH OF MAZZINI.

IT is with profound grief that we chronicle
to-day the death of JOSENI MAZZINT. A
truly great man has passed away from earth.
A life of toil and sacrifice has closed. A great
destiny has been accomplished. But though,
at the present moment, we feel saddened by
our loss, we feel also the gratifying conscious-
ness that the great aim of his life—the unity
of Italy—had found, previous to his death, an
almost complete fulfilment.
In him the highest Mats Of life were sus-
tained by an ardent faith, an indomitable will,
and an unflagging energy. And in him was
found a lofty genius which kindled all hearts,
and inspired all honest souls. He found Italy,
as Earl RUSSELL cynically expressed it, "a
geographical idea," and left it a nation—not all
that he wished, but more than any one, at the
commencement of his career, dared to hope.
He found it divided and infested. by filthy
swarms of little sovereigns, who, with their
hungry parasites degraded and preyed upon
it. He evoked a spirit that hunted them out,,
and east them off for ever. He taught the
young men of Italy their duty, and called on
them to perform it, and they answered to
,f,ris
call, and gave themselves freely to their noun-
try—
Sowing their lives for her seed,
That the ir . dust might rebuild her,—a nation,
That, the ir souls :night re-light her,—a star.
And now, when called away to his rest, he has
left it united, under one head, still awaiting
hopefully the . day when the Law shall be
accepted as sovereign, and the Nation shall
live its own life, master of itself.

He found Italy in spiritual thraldom, under
the feet of an ignorant and. intolerant priest-
hood, with its capital the centre and sit* of
priestly corruption. He has left it more than
half through a process of purgation, Whieh
promises to be thorough and complete. The
Papacy, which waled to defy time, and.
work out its ends in utter disregard of n'
human authority, is now trying to make up
its mind to take itself away from Itome, and
to find a home elsewhere, as a favour conferred
in pity and charity.
All this MAZZENI accomplished under perse-
cution," in disregard of slander," in exile, and
with obstacles of various kinds opposed to
him, before which any spirit less gifted than
his would have sunk. No life has been leo
a failure than his ; no life in the present
century has been richer in great results.
And what he has done is only a portion of his
great work. His life was rich in fruitful
work, but he has left behind. him Books from
which the world will yet reap a glorious
harvest. Those who would struggle success-
fully for the improvement of their fell0w0)

will find their strength in his pages. They
will find it there stated with eloquence and
force, and, above all, with a sincerity which
none can doubt, how high and holy a thing

duty is, and. how necessary as a forerunner
and sustainer of all human right. "We
must," he says, "convince men that they are
all sons of one sole Clop, and bound to fulfil
and execute one solo law here on earth; that
each of them is bound to live, not for himself,
but for others ; that the aim of existence is
not to be more or less happy, but to make
themselves and others more virtuous ; that to
struggle against injustice and error, wherever
they exist, in the name and for the benefit of
their brothers, is not only a right but a duty—a
duty which may not be neglected without sin
—the duty of their whole life."

Thus 111a2uNi laboured in life ; in his
defence we have nothing to say. When any
evil done by him has been alleged on proof
against him, when the charges that have been
made over and over again struggle out of
the murky region of slander into that of
sober inquiry, it will be time enough for his
friends to take up his defence. Now we have
only time for sorrow for the loss of the great
ard suffering man just passed away. Ac-
knowledging with gratit tide his noble services—
All thy whole life's love, thine heart's whole,
Thou bust given as who gives gladly, 0 thou the
strut:mil soul.

But he has gone to his rest, and now the
slanderers will be for a time silent. There
are few, even of these, who do not stand
abashed in the presence of death. In a little
time the triumph of his principles will justify
his life. The men of Italy, the women of
Italy, even the children will receive into
their lives the influence of his spirit, and
these will influence those who govern there,
and thus the wild dream of the sorrowful
dreamer, the hope clung to by the noble exile
who never despaired of his country, will
become the daily life of Italy.
Let us thank GOD, then, for the man who
was brave, Rua true, and wise, and earnest,
and resolute ; and let us remember in our
sorrow how much the value is of one grand
life, and how all-powerful the genius of the
one in lifting the many to an appreciation of, and
struggle after whatever elevates and ennobles
lire. Not for success, not for reward—

'Tis not the grapes of Canaan that repay,
But the high faith, that failed not by the way ;
This lesson he taught us, and even though
his life had been as complete a failure as it
has been a success, we see in his personal
sufforing and his death, as it were in exile,
that duty is duty, and that because right is
right, to follow right is " wisdom in the scorn
of consequence."

THE POLITIONL LUTHER.

PRINCE BTSMARCK is a player who never
Bits down to political chess without putting his
adversary into a corner. He is now fairly
committed to a contest with the clerical power,
and he does not disguise his intention to push
the fight to a final issue. The battle has
turned hitherto upon the question of inspec-
tion of the public schools of Germany. Here.
tofore this function has been in the hands of
the clergy, who, in Germany, are partly
Lutheran, or Protestant, and partly Roman
Catholic. The latter section have in a manner
ccupired against the head ruler, under the
RueEtton, of the Fatherland. It is necessary
to his influence, and to his influence for
undoubted good, that he should confound their
rind frustrate their knavish tricks.
the
therefore announced his resolution to take
education of the people from under their
unsafe protection. But he could not do this
With reference to them alone. The thing
laud be done with regard to the whole body
of the clergy, Protestant as well as Romanist,
0! it could not be done at all. This seemed
!like involving the innocent in the same eon-
. emnation with the guilty. It might, indeed,
be Raid, that wholesome principle required the
subject to be taken wholly out of the care of
the ministers of religion; but this doctrine
InLe likely to be as unpopular with the
Lutheran portion as it was distasteful to the
papist.
Nevertheless, the CHANCELLOR has sue.
Seeded. In the House of Representatives his
Bill passed by no larger a majority than 26 ;

whereas, in the House of Nobles, it has been
carried by a majority of 49. The nobles were
reluctant, and opinion among the people was
greatly divided; but the MINISTER showed
himself resolute, and his policy found greater
support where it was ,to be expected that it
would have the least. Even the EMPEROR
hesitated, and some other members of the
Court did more than hesitate ; but Prince
BISMARCK was determined, and before the
determined man difficulties fell back and dis-
appeared. His Imperial MASTER, it is under.
stood, yielded to his exposition of the political
necessity, and even consented to the creation
of as many new peers as might be wanted
for the purpose. The menace has proved
enough, and the Rouse, as it was, furnished
the required majority.
The policy is a bold one, but none other
ever yet succeeded against such a class of
antagonists. As for the schools, these, now,
in place of being inspected by priests, will be
'put under the supervision of State officials,
who will be laymen. So far, then, as the
education of the German people is concerned,
this is a highly important measure ; especially
in Prussian Poland, where the anti-
Prussian influence and efforts of the
Romish clergy had made a radical change
politically indispensable. Both there and
in Southern Germany, where Popery is in
the ascendant, the action of the MINISTER
will no doubt rouse the auger of the priest-
hood to the utmost. But he will have counted
the cost; and among the Protestants, and yet
more among the Indifferentists in religion,
whom we suspect to be numerous and powerful,
he will have created or revived a spirit which
will mightily aid his policy, when, as it now
must, it takes the clear direction of free
thought and unfettered expression of opinion. ,
The priests, of course, will never forgive the
man who conquered Austria, because that
Power was thereby reduced to the necessity of
breaking with Rome, and of adopting that
Liberal home policy which has changed the
most monarchical of monarchies into one of
the most constitutional of representative
governments. The yet more complete humi-
liation of France, with the total destruction
of the Napoleonic Empire and dynasty, has
afforded to the emissaries of ambitious Popery
greatly increased reason to look Upon Germany
as once more the seat of a power irreconcilably
adverEe to principles and :wimples having for
their object the subjugation of nations and
their rulers to the sway of a sacerdotal caste.

The effect of firmness and resolution on the
part of Germany, will be manifest over all
Europe. Even Russia can have but little
sympathy in an opposition to the teaching of
the German language in Prussian Poland
which is under the direction of the Latin
Church. For, in the governing powers of
Russia, Muscovite is hindered from having
full play by the Teutonic element which pre-
dominates in the administration. The Cz.t.n
is too much of a Pope himself both in Church
and in State, to take complacency in any
movements anywhere directed from Rome.
In fact, the secular power everywhere, whether
princely or popular, either has shaken off the
sacerdotal yoke, or is seeking to do so. By
the policy which Prince Ilfsauncx has now
so openly declared, ho has effected more than
the sword has accomplished or could ever
achieve ; and the intrepid monk who defied
the Pun and burned his Bull did not acquire
a fame wider or more lasting than may yet
attach itself to the name and deeds of this
Political LUTII.EIt.

articles.title: TIM RELIGIOUS DIFFICULTY.
articles.text:
TIM RELIGIOUS DIFFICULTY.

TAE Religious Difficulty in regard to
education has boon grappled with and dis-
posed of by the Lancashire Presbytery of the
United Presbyterians. The locality of this
voluntary Church court gives interest, if not
importance also, to its proceedings in so public
and so vexed a question. It was first proposed
that they should insist upon the Bible as the
foundation of all true knowledge, and thou,
limiting the duty of the State to. enabling the
children to read that book, leave it to the
different religious bodies "to apply that
power to the acquisition of Bible truth." To
this, by way of amendment, it was moved, in
order to be mote explicit and decided, that

religious instruction is a necessary part of
education, but that, since the State cannot
undertake to give it without violating the
rights of conscience and the principle of
religious equality, the only way is for the
State to establish a thoroughly national sys-
tem of secular instruction, leaving instruction
in religion entirely in the hands of parents
and of the Christian Church. A second
amendment was proposed, founded upon the
difficulty of dealing with the case of parents
indifferent to religion; but, after discussion,
the original motion and the second amendment
were both withdrawn, and the first amend-
ment, with modifications, was unanimously
adopted. The result was a resolution which,
beginning with the recognition of the supreme
importance and absolute need of religious in-
struction, and insisting upon every child being
taught to read the Bible, but admitting that
the teaching of religion cannot be undertaken
by the State, in accordance with religious
freedom and equality, ended with declaring
it to be the only wise and satisfactory action
on the put of the State to establish a
thoroughly national system of secular educa-
tion, and to leave the religious instruction of
the people entirely in the hands of the parents
and of the Christian Church. This appears
to us to be as clear and as just a solution of
the difficulty as the art of man could devise
or suggest.

articles.title: STEAM BOILER EXPLOSIONS.
articles.text:
STEAM BOILER EXPLOSIONS.

TILE yearly meeting of the steam-users in
Manchester has brought out a number of in-
structive facts. The Report showed that the
year had not elapsed in idleness. Nearly six
thousand boilers had been more or less over-
hauled. The first dtty of 1872 saw them in
possession of a total guarantee fund of more
than £21,000. "No explosion," says the Re-
port, "occurred to any boiler under inspec-
tion during the whole year." On the other'
hand, it came to the knowledge
,of the Cotn-:
mittee that to boilers not under inspection,
there had occurred 51 explosions, killing 50
persons, and injuring 107 others—a less less o 4
life, however, than in any other recent year. In
accordance with the Select Committee of the
House of Commons, the Association finds that
coroners' inquests are inadequate to such in-
quiries, and that most explosions arc attribut-
able to avoidable causes, such as malconstruc-
lion, insufficient fittings, and so forth. The
Parliamentary Committee had, however, been
led to one conclusion.in which the experience
of the Association does not enable them to
concur. Instead of finding that many explo-
sions arise from causes not to be 'prevented by
periodical inspection, they are convinced from
experience that such an inspection as that
enjoyed by their own members, would, if made
universal, make boiler explosions very infre-
quent. They object, moreover, to the recom-
mendations of the House of Commons Com-
mittee as going to punish after the fad, instead
of preventing its recurrence.
Sir Wfm,Lot FirunUliN, the able Presi-
dent of this important Association, stated, as
the result of experiments, that, by the use of
dry steam, at a high pressure, and totally
disconnected from water, a much inoreased
rate of expansion could be gained with perfect
safety, and a great economy of fuel, as well as
a reduced expense in the making of machinery.
"The time," lie said, "was not far distant
when manufacturers would turn out their
goods at a reduction of one half, or perhaps
more, upon the present cost."
With regard to explosions, Mr. HUGH
MAsom, though himself a cotton-spinner,
strongly advocated the compulsory inspection
of all steam boilers, and, on his motion, an
outspoken resolution was unanimously carried,
in harmony with the facts and views developed ,
in the Report of the Committee.

articles.title: MR. GOLDWIN SMITH ON MR. GLAD-
articles.text:
MR. GOLDWIN SMITH ON MR. GLAD-

STONE.

A good deal of time and energy seems to be frit-
tered away in mere House-of-Commons bickerings
with Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone's position is
surely one of which we may take a philosophic
view. Ile is, as he alwa3B has been, greatly under
aristocratical and ecclesiastical influence; the men
with whom he lives, and whom he naturally loves
to promote, are the members of an aristocratic and
High Church circle, he has bound himself to the
maintenance of the House of Lords and of the
State Church, and has thereby morally closed his
legislative career. But he has at the same time
real popular sympathies, which have led him to do
more than any other statesman of the present day
in the line of fiscal and economical reform for the
improvement of the people, and has drawn upon
him the bitter and almost delirious hatred of the
people's worst enemies. Not
,to support him
against those enemies would have been foolish and
culpable pessimism. He has proved* himself a
hearty and courageous reformer of abuses; his sin-
cerity gave us the extension of the suffrage; to him
we owe the Irish Church Bill and the Irish Land
Bill. He is at least as liberal as his Parliament,
which is thoroughly plutocratic, and had ex-
hausted its Liberalism when it had redeemed its
election pledges on the subject of the Irish Church
and Land. The worst of his measures, and that
most indicative of what a Liberal would call the
weak side of his character, the Education Bill, by
which national education has been thrown
back into the hands of the priest party, was
mano3uvred through Parliament by the member
for what we always deemed the eminently and
staunchly Liberal constituency of Bradford, who
is now receiving the deserved mood of cloaca].
applause. Not much more will be obtained from
Mr. Gladstone, but how anything more is to be
obtained by taking the executive government from
him and giving it to the leaders of the oligarchy,
it is difficult to see.—Mr. Goldwin Smith in the
Fortnightly. Review for March.

nu TRADE UNION LEGISLATION OF

LAST YEAR.

There are some rumours, to which we attach
but little faith, that the Government intends this
year to introduce a general measure, repealing part
of the legislation of last year, and otherwise deal.
ing with the whole subject of master and servant.
Government, apparently, has plenty to do to
carry out oven the rather meagre programme an-
nounced at the beginning of the session, without
undertaking so large a matter as a general Bill on
the whole relationship of capital and labour.
besides, if such a measure had been intended, it
certainly would have been referred to in the
Queen's Speech, or would have been announced
before this in reply to one of those convenient
questions that ministers know how to get asked as
well as how to answer.

But if Government will not do anything in this
matter we may be sure that an effort will be made
by other parties to interfere with the settlement
effected by lust year's Acts. It will be remembered
that at the Trade Union Congress, held a short
time ago at Nottingham, a committee of unionists
and their friends—called the Parliamentary Com-
mittee—was appointed, chiefly with a view of
getting the Criminal Law Amendment Act re-
pealed. This Committee has, since the Nottingham
meeting, been sitting in London, and has been very
busy. The usual tactics are being pursued. In-
dividual members of Parliament are being inter-
viewed, primed, and pledged.

At a mootingof the Committee, held on the 17th
of last mouth, the secretary reported " that several
members of Parliament had been seen with re-
ferenco to the Criminal Law -kntendment Act, and
the other questions referred to the Committee.
Mr. Vernon Harcourt bad been seen with a view
to induce him to undertake the question of repeal-
ing the Act passed last session. He expressed Ms

willingness to do everything in his power to meet
the wishes of the Committee. At a subsequent
interview at the hon. gentleman's house, at which
Mr. McDonald and the secretary were present, he
requested the Committee to supply him with all the
facts relative to the prosecutions under the Act, to
enable him to present a clear case to the House,
and he intimated that he thought the most effec-
tive way would be for him to propose a resolution
to the House, and thereby get an expression of
opinion on the subject. This, he thought, would
be more effective than for a private member to
bring in a Bill, which would be put off from time
to time."

It is therefore evident that it behoves us and
all friends of free labour to be making prepara-
tions to meet this movement. We accordingly
ask our readers to furnish us with all information
on the subject that is in their possession. And at
the 53.m0 time let every opportunity be taken of
furnishing members of Parliament with the ma-
terials whereupon to found a just estimate of the
whole movement. In all this no time must be
lost. We therefore again ask our readers for as-
sistance in carry,ing out the resolution arrived at
by the builders' meeting at Manchester in January
last.—Bullelers' Trade Circular.

articles.title: HALFPENNY POSTAL CARDS.
articles.text:
HALFPENNY POSTAL CARDS.

The explanation given by Mr. Baxter of the
change which has just been made in the arrange-
ments about postal cards is a good illustration of
the differences which have often occurred in the
actual development of improvements from the
expectations formed of them; When postal cards
were established Government took the matter into its
own hand, and sold the cards at a halfpenny each,
charging nothing for paper, but allowing none but
Government cards to pass through the post. The
expectation certainly was that the cards, whatever
their other uses, would be largely used by the
poor, and would be bought singly or in quantities
of less than a dozen, so that no charge for paper
could well be made. In actual experience this has
not been the case. The dealing in the cards has
been almost exclusively wholesale, the chief
use made of them, we believe, having been for
business circulars, partly, but far from wholly, as a
mode of advertising. For these reasons, and not
merely to meet the grievance of stationers, who
complained that Government was invading their
private trade by not making a distinct charge for
postage, the Government has resolved to change its
arrangements, and adapt them td the busin as s
which has grown up. The sales being exclusiv oly
wholesale, a charge for paper can and will be made
by the Government in addition to postage, and
private cards will be allowed under certain restric-
tions for the postage of a halfpenny. We may
anticipate in consequence a speedy. development of
the postal card system, and so great is the business
already that the department will gain £13,000 by
charging an extra halfpenny for each dozen of
postal cards.

articles.title: NEW LICENSING BILL.
articles.text:
THE NEW LICENSING BILL.

It is stated that the Now Licensing 13111 has
been printed, though it has not yet been laid be-
fore Parliament by the Government, nor placed in
the hands of Members generally. We do not
know on what authority the statement is made,
and the coarse which the Government is said to
have taken, in handing a bill of this kind to a
44 privileged few," is certainly a very unusual one.
We deal with the statement, therefore, subject to
the reserve thus suggested. The bill, as sketched
out by the correspondent who communicates the
statement to a contemporary, is not a very complex
one. There is to be no attempt to remodel the
licensing system, and the more serious provisions
of the bill of last year apparently disappear alto.
gether. The licensing jurisdiction is to remain
where it is at-present, with the magistrates, but
no magistrate is to adjudicate who is connected
directly or indirectly with the traffic. The bill, in
fact, is directed chiefly to the regulation of the
traffic, by restricting the boars of sale, and by
making the fines for offences under the Act more
stringent. In some cases the sale of liquors is to
he restricted within the hours of seven, n.m. and

Iten p.m. Nothing is said as to the continuance of
' the Suspensory Act, and without this it is certain
that the bill thus sketched will not meet the
difficulty. There must be no power, save under
special circumstances, defined in the Act, to in-
crease the number of licenses, or the bill will only
touch the fringes of the evil. For ourselves we
wish to see the licenses reduced, and at least we
should demand that they should not be increased.
The restriction of the hours of sale, combined
with more stringent police regulatl3nB and a more
strict enforcement of them, would be a great
boon, but if the bill stopped there it would fall
short of that which the public expects, and that
which it desires.

articles.title: DEATH OF MAZZINI.
articles.text:
DEATH OF MAZZINI.

A telegram from Paris announces the death,
at Pisa, of Joseph ltazzini, who, a few days
since, was reported to be preparing a revolu-
tionary invasion of Italy in the Canton of
Ticino.

Mazzini, one of the most remarkable men of
modern Italy, was born in 1808, at Genoa, his
father being a physician of note, of good
private means. In youth, Mazzini was noted
for the warmth of his friendships, the fixity of
his will, and the exaggerated susceptibility of
his human feelings. From birth, sentiments
of social equality were engendered in him by
the example of his parents; and very early
tho degraded political condition of his country
began to prey upon his mind, producing
ardent aspirations for her national unity and
deliverance from foreign domination, which
seemed to him attainable only through a return
to the Republican glories of ancient times.
Mazzini's patriotic enthusiasm speedily gained
absolute sway over his spirit, and led him to
renounce his cherished idea of a life of litera-
ture and contemplative study, for the action
and strife of the political arena. In 1827 his
maiden essay in literature, " Amor Patrio
di Dante," appeared in the Liberal journal,
the Subalpino; and he subsequently contri-
buted critical, literary, and political papers to
the Antologia of Florence and the Indicatory
Genovese. In the pages of this latter
originally appeared the essay subsequently re-
published under the title of" Scritti d' un Italian°
Vivente." Literature, according to Mazzini's
own assertion, having been employed by the
Liberal party solely as a means for the great
end of Liberal propagandism, the journals
were suppressed, and the writers disbanded.
In 1830 the affiliation of Mazzini to the secret
society of the Carbonari was the introductory
step to his practical political career ; and the
young member, was speedily invested
.with a
preponderating influence in the councils and
missions .of the body. Ensnared and betrayed
by a Piedmontese spy, Mazzini was arrested,
detained for six months in the fortress of
Savona, and finally liberated on condition of
his departure from Italy. After short resi-
dences in several places, he took up his abode
in Marseilles, and thence he addressed to
Charles Albert his famous letter, which drew
down on the daring young writer
.a decree of
perpetual banishment. The organization of a
new Liberal league, "Young Italy," was
Mazzini's next work. Republican and
unionist to the core, the tendencies of this
groat body were more humanitarian and
universal than its extinct predecessor, Car-
bonarism. In addition to the paramount aim
of Italy's republican union under one common ,
law, and the extinction of foreign rule, the '
general principles of this new association
enforced the universal obligation to labour for
a common moral regeneration, and the esta-
blishment of political equality over the world.
Liberty, equality, and humanity were the
watchwords of the body; "God. and the
People" their motto; white, red, mid green
their tricoloured banner ; education and
insurrection the great agencies of their opera-
tions ;. assassination was erased from their
statutes, and. the symbolic dagger of the
Carbonari was replaced by the more humane
emblems of a book and the cypress.
Mazzini was the animating spirit of this
formidable league, which speedily inclosed all
Europe in a network of similar associations,
modified to meet the individual require-
month of the various European nationalities.
Banishment from Marseilles, in consequence
of the extensive operations of the society
having been revealed to the authorities, com-
pelled Mazzini to resort to concealment for a
period of several months. About this time, a
charge was brought against him of advocating
assassination as a legitimate weapon in the
warfare of liberalism; but the charge was
proved in the public tribunals of France to be
false; and in the British Parliament (1845)
Sir
.James Graham made an apology to M az-
zmi. for having re-echoed the calumny. The
first-fruits of La Giovine Italia was the
revolutionary expedition of Savoy, organised
by Mazzini at Geneva, but which was defeated
by the royal troops. Sentence of death, par
contzonace, was recorded against Mazzini, in
the Sardinian courts, for his participation in
the affair; but he soon recommenced with
increased vigour his revolutionary operations.
A new association, entitled "New Europe,"
and based on principles of European rights
and enfranchisement, was inaugurated by the
exertions of Mazzini in Switzerland. In 1837
Mazzini quited Switzerland for England, and
finally took up his abode in London. From
thence, his labours in the Italian revolutionary
cause have been incessant. To trace the part
enacted by Mazzini in the great crisis of 1848
, would be to record the history of that period,
so intimately were his isdividual acts connected
with the course of events. The resolute com-
batant of partial union and monarchical leader-
ship at Milan, Mazzini retired to Switzerland
on the capitulation of Milan to the Aus-
trians to reappear in Florence on the rising of
Tuscany, and finally
.at Rome, where he was
elected triumvir amidst the triumphant re -
joioings of the capital of Italy. His tenure
of. supreme authority was marked by sue h
wisdom, moderation, and success, as to elicit

a public tribute of approbation from Lord
Palmerston. On the surrender of Rome, by
Mazzini's advice, he quitted the city, and pros
ceeded to Lausanne, via Marseilles. The
conduct of France he bitterly attacked in
public letters to De Tocqueville and others.
He subsequently returned to London, and, at
his instigation, risings in Milan (1853) and in
Piedmont (1857) were attempted. in 1859,
while lending the whole weight of his influenee
to the revolutionary movements going . on
in Italy, he combated with vigilant foresight
the threatened French predominance, and
refused to accord faith to the liberalprogramme,
of Louis Napoleon. The Sicilian expedition
of 1860 owed as much to the organisation of
Mazzini as to the heroic command of Gari-
baldi. In the more recent attempt which
ended in the inauspicious engagement of
Aspromonte, the two leaders were somewhat
at variance as to the most efficient plan of
attack, Rome beins. preferred . by Garibaldi,
while Venice was deemed the most vulnerable
point by Mazzini.
In the beginning of 1861, an endeavour was
made to implicate Mazzini in the attempt of
four Italians to assassinate the French Em-
peror, one of the criminals having on his trial
affirmed that he had given him money and•
explosive bombs. At the trial it was also stated
by the Procureur-Imperial that a paper had been
found in the possession of one of the accused
persons, directing him to write for money to
a Mr. Flowers, at 35, Thurloe-square, Bramp-
ton, "where," the Procureur added, "a mem-
ber of the English Parliament resided, who,
in 1855, had baen appointed banker to the
Tibaldi conspirators. As Mr. Stansfeld,
then Junior Lord of the Admiralty, resided at
the address indicated, this statement was
supposed to implicate him in the conspiracy,
and the matter was brought before the House
of Commons, first by Mr. Cox, M.P. for Fins-
bury, and afterwards by Sir Henry Stracey,
who moved: 'That the speech of the Pro-
cureur -Imperial, on the trial of Greco, impli-
cating a member of this House and of her
Majesty's Government in the plot for the
assassination of our ally the Emperor of the
French, deserves the serious consideration of
this House." Mr. Stansfeld indignantly
denied all knowledge of Greco or of *r•
Flowers, but admitted that he had been 011
intimate terms with Mazzini for eighteen
years, and affirmed his conviction that no man
had over been more cruelly or wrongfully
maligned than he had been. Lord Palmerston,
then Prime Minister, accepted Mr. Stansfeld 's
explanation, which ho deemed perfectly satis-
factory, but Sir Henry Stracey's motion was
pushed to a division, and negatived by only
ten votes, the mumbers being—for, 161;
against, 171. There was a manifest deter-
mination, however, to pursue the subject, and
Mr. Stansfeld tend9red the resignation of his
post at the Admiralty, which was only no
cepted by the Prime Minister after consider-
able hesitation and delay.
In December, 1866, Mazzini issued a pro-
clamation to the Italian people urging them to
ooneentrate their attentien on Rome. "Rome,"
he said, "represents the mission of Italy
among the nations; the word of our people;
the eternal gospel of unification to the peoples.
Can I hid her annex herself as a subaltern,
and an appendix to Florence? Can I, without
profanation, counsel Rome to give the conse-
cration of her prestige to a dying institution,
and throw the gigantic shadow of her glory
over the errors, the crimes, the servility to the
foreigner, of a monarchy which uttered no
word of protest for you during your eighteen
years of slavery; and which has declared by
the lips of its Ministers, We never will go
to Rome unless by the permission of Franee
and the Pope?' No; Rome ought never to
annex herself to Florence; we are all bound
to annex ourselves to Rome. The material
unity of Italy is nearly complete. All that
we want is a symbol to represent that moral
unity which can only be realised by the Re-
public. What we now have is the body, svitll-
- the soul. We await the soul from Hemet!
but Rome can only inspire the inert form witu
soul on condition of preserving herself pure
from the defilement by which it is now 00e"
taminated. Should Rome accept that, Rome,
too, would fail; and with her, for I know net
how long, the grand destiny of Italy in
Europe." Since the time when this manifesto
was issued, Mazzini has lived a life of com"
partitive obscurity, and it is rather singular
that the improbable rumour of his being en-
gaged in. preparing a revolutionary invasion
of Italy in the canton of Ticino should eo
soon be followed by the announcement of hie
death at Pisa.
Mazzillitß writings are various and extensiVe
and include valuable dissertations on Art'
literature, and music, in which he is a Pr°-
ficient. Ho founded several Liberal journals,
and contributed able papers to variell;
British periodicals. His valuable narration 0
the insurrection of Milan, " Cenni e Doi;n:
menti Intorno all' Insurrezione Lombardo, Ewe'
Guerra Resia del 1848," has been translated
into French and English, under the title,
"Royalty and Republicanism in Italy.
elevation of sentiment, and the flashing 010-
quence of his writings, have exerted en
immense influence on the fervid youth of ItelY:
A complete;edition of Mazsini's works, editeu,

by Daelli, and corrected by Mazzini himself,
has been published. Whatever may be thought
of. Mazzini's political views (observes
"Chambers," from whom we have quoted
above), few will call in question the ardent
sincerity of his patriotism. Still less can we
refuse to admire the inflexibility with which
he has pursued his aim, unchecked by perse-
cution, calumny, and defeat. Mazzini pos-
sesses in the highest degree that personal
fascination, by which friends are converted
into ardent partisans. In his private life, he
is allowed to be a model of purity and frugal
simplicity, as in his public career he has been
conspicuous for disinterestedness and self-
abnegation; and to these peronal virtues of
Mazzini, aided by his extraordinary influence
and eloquence, those who know Italy best
ascribe a, great share at least in inspiring that
higher tone of life manifest in recent yearS
among the Italian youth, without which the.
political regeneration of the country would
have been impossible.

articles.title: TRUCK BILL
articles.text:
THE TRUCK BILL

The Government Bill to amend the law
with respect to the payment of wages to work-
men in certain trades applies exclusively to all
oceupations to which the Coal Mines Regu-
lation Bill and Metalliferous Mines Bill of
this Session are applicable, or the Factory
Acts or Workshops Acts. In relation to these
occupations the Bill provides that the whole
of a workman's wages shall be paid in coin of
the realm without any deduction, and without
any condition as to the spending thereof; but
a payment may be made in bank notes with
the workman's consent, or (if above X 5) by an
uncrossed check on a banker carrying on
business not more than five miles off. The
Wages are to be paid at intervals not exceeding
a week, except where the contract specially
provides for the payment then of only a part,
not being less than 90 per cent. the unpaid
balance to be paid within four weeks. Stipu-
lations made in contravention of this
enactment will not be binding upon the work-
man. No wages are to be paid on premises
licensed for the sale of any intoxicating liquor,
or at any office, yard, road, or. place belonging
or contiguous to such premises, or on any
premises on which goods are ordinarily sold to
the workman. If goods have been snpplied
to a workman by his master or his master's
agent as or on account of his wages, or at any
shop in the profits of which such master or
agent has any interest, no action can be
brouilit against the workman in respect of
such goods, nor a set-off maintained in any
proceeding by the workman for his wages.
But the Bill will not apply to deductions
allowed by any statute from children's wages
in respeot of, their school fees, and a contract
for the deduction of money for the education
of the children of workmen will be legal;
neither will the Bill apply to deductions for
board and lodging of a person living in the
same house with the master, or to contracts
for deduction of a fine from wages. The
accounts of the expenditure of sums deducted
for education of workmen's children are to be
audited annually by auditors appointed by the
workmen. A workman is not to assign, en-
cumber, or charge his wages before they are
payable, or give any authority to another to
receive them; the assignment, &c., will be
void. It will be an offence against this Bill
for a master or his agent to make any. con-
tract with or impose any condition on or use
any compulsion towards a workman as to the
place at which, or the manner in which, or
the person with whom wages shall be expended.
The term " contract' in this Bill includes any
'understanding, device, Bzo., or arrangement
Whatsoever, direct or indirect, and whensoever
made. The punishment for offences against
this Bill is by penalty, not exceeding £2O, to
be recovered by summary conviction, subje. ot
to appeal to the Quarter Sessions. The in-
spectors of factories and of mines are to enforce
. the provisions of the Bill in England; in
Scotland the procurators fiscal. - The Secre-
tary of State may at any time, where the
exigencies of any particular case or class of
oases make it expedient, grant temporary ex-
emptions from the above provisions with re-
spent to the time at which wars are to be
13.1", or the allowance of certain deductions
therefrom.
