articles.title: ENIPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN IN , B,RICKMAKING.
articles.text:
THE ENIPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN IN
, B,RICKMAKING.

On Friday afternoon a deputation, mom-
panied by Mr. S. R. Graves, M.P., and Mr.
Rathbone, M.P., members for Liverpool, had
an interview with Mr. Bruce, at the Home-
office, on the subject of the employment of
children at the brick-yards. The deputation
consisted for the most part of master and
operative brickmakers from Liverpool, Birken-
head, and Blackburn, and the purpose was to
see whether Mr. Bruce would consent to a
modification of, the ,Factory and Workshops
Act, so as to enable briekmakers to employ
boys from the age of twolve years instead of
fourteen years. The deputation presented a
petition numerously signed by master and
operative builders and brickmaKers. It was
asked that as brickmaking was only carried
on during the summer months the master
might be allowed to employ boys of the age
of twelve years on full time. The education
of the children,, it was urged, could be
attended to during the winter months, when
briekmaking-was not carried on. Mr. Bruce,
in reply to the various points urged by the
deputation, and in answer to questions put by
Mr. Graves and Mr. Rathbone, said he had no
power to authorise. the employraentof children
under twelve during the long hours of labour
described as" full time." A. special clause had
been introduced into the Act to meet health-
ful out-door employments, such as brick-
making was represented to be, and the master,
briokmakers were really better situated than
the owners of factories. Power was given to
work children three days a week, and children
could be worked a certain number of hours
each day. If the master-brickmakers expe-
rienced difficulty in obtaining relays it was
really, a matter which could not be helped.
The Factory Act, no doubt, interfered with
labour, but on the whole it was found to work
advantageously, and to the decided benefit of
young persons. It was certain that the House
of Commons would not grant any further re-
laxation of the regulations under the Act
which were at present in fem. in answer to
a question by .Mr. Rathbone, Mr. Bruce said
he, had no power to authorise the employment
of
,children at full time for four instead of
three days a week.

articles.title: LAMBETH a° OL OF ART.
articles.text:
LAMBETH a° OL OF ART.

On Friday night the distribution of prizes
to the students of this verTsucoessful institu-
tion was made by Canon Gregory, at the
school, Miller's-lane, Upper Kennington-lane.
Miss Agnes Schenk was awarded the gold
medal for design for lace, and also received
the Prince of Wales' scholarship of £26. The
silver medallists were Miss Alice Purkess,
for a hoad from life; Mr. Arthur Barlow,
for a model from the antique; and Mr. Tom
Hunt, for a life study. There were seven
bronze medals, and numerous other prizes,
including books, money, and several useful
articles. Canon Gregory, before the presenta-
tion' which took up a good deal of time,
sketched the eighteen years' history of the
academy, from its modest origin, with which
he was personally connected, to its present
handsome, useful, and large proportions. The
aim of its feunders and existing managers
was to render the teaching a practical adjunct
to the iron and pottery industries of the dis-
trict. How far they had succeeded might be
gathered from the works exhibited so plenti-
fully on all sides of the room. This was the
first occasion of the pupils being able to dis-
play beautiful objects of pottery art of their
own conception and workmanship, a result
due in great measure to the liberality of Mr.
Henry Doulton, and the zeal, taste, and ability
of Mr. Sparks, the headmaster. The distri-
bution of the evening was for two years,
owing to the rebuilding and enlargement of
the premises, and he appealed to the overflow-
ing audience before him to Contribute some-
thing towards wiping off a debt of £3OO this
extension had left unpaid. Mr. Tom Taylor,
the eminent critic and dramatist, after the
distribution, recited an address upon Art,
taking for his leading theme the street decora-
tions of the recent Thanksgiving Day. Specu-
lating upon the unfavourable impression they
must have produced upon the minds of the
youthful Japanese sent over to study our
habits tastes, and institutions, and who were
in SC Paul's on the day, he thought they
must have said to themselves this could not
be the England of 600 years ago, of which
they had read, or the country that set so high
a value upon the beautiful productions of
their own Japan. In this strain he reasoned,
contending that the art taste of the nation had
degenerated, but argued that institutions of
this kind wore destined to restore correct
notions amongst the people of the picturesque.
The subsequent proceedings embraced com-
plimentary votes to Canon Gregory, Mr. Tom
Taylor, and Mr. Sparks, the headmaster,
which were very heartily accorded.

articles.title: LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.
articles.text:
LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

The weekly meeting of this Board was held
Wednesday in the Council Chamber,Guildhall.
Lord Lawrence presided.
On the motion of Lord Lawrence, the day
for the Marylebone election was changed from
the 25th to the 28th March next, and the day
for the Finsbury election was altered from the
2nd of April to the 3rd of April.
Respecting compulsory education, on the
7th February- last the School Management
Committee reported the action they had taken
upon a circular from the Education Depart-
ment with reference to the issue of certificates
to scholars under Bye-law 4. The last para-
graph of the circular stated that it was left to
the Board to provide for the issue of certificates
to seholars not attending public elementary
schools. The clerk was instructed to com-
municate with Sir 'Francis Sandford, stating
that the words used in. section 74 of the
Elementary Education Act seemed to preclude
the Board from testing, by their own inspectors,
the acquirements of such children. The com-
mittee received a reply from Sir Francis
Sandford, Stating that the words of the statute
neither threw upon the department the res-
ponsibility of granting a Certifieate in any
particular case, nor did they prevent the
Board from testing, in whatever manner they
thought best, the reasonableness of any excuse
offered for non-attendance at 8611°01 of a child
Who had reached a certain standard Of
education.

The Rev. J. Rodgers here brought up a re-
port from the Bye-laws Committee, stating
that the committee did not consider it desir-
able to take any action in the matter at pre-
sent. It had, however, ordered the following
notice to parents and others who have charge
of children, to be printed for circulation:
"The School Board is empowered to compel
the parents of children of from five to thirteen
years of age to send them to school, unless
there is reasonable excuse. There are now
numerous vacancies in existing schools. The
School Board therefore give notice that parents
of children who are absent from school without
suflioient reason are liable to a penalty, and
that steps will be taken to carry out the law."
Lord Lawrence, as there was now a break in
the proceedings, rose and said :—Gentlemen,
I take this opportunity of making a few obser-
vations respecting the state of my health, and
the necessity which obliges me to sever myself
for a time from the Board. I about to take
advantage of the leave of absence which you
have so kindly and courteously accorded to
me. I take advantage of that leave of absence
with, I can assure you, the greatest disinclina-
tion. I have a strong wish to remain with
the Board, so as to see the work which we
have undertaken make progresie---and I have
i endeavoured to assist n that work as fir as
has been in my power. (Hear, hear, and ap-
plause.) I am especially desirous of doing so at
present, now that the Board has began to go
faster than hitherto.. I feel bound, however,
not to go against the advice of my medical
friends. It is therefore incumbent on me to
retire from the business of the Board for some
time. During the first year's existence of the
Board, I was careful to attend regularly the
committee meetings of the Board; but of late
I have not been able to do so. I feel that I
can no longer bear the strain of work which is
incumbent upon the chairman of such a
Board as this. I have, therefore, reluctantly
come to the conclusion that I should give up,
and endeavour to make an attempt to recruit
my health. I earnestly hope that my absence
will be only for a short time. (Hear, hear,
and, applause.) It is my desire to come back
before long, and to resume my position at the
Board. Nothing would have been more
gratifying to me than to be able to remain at
my post without any interruption to carry out
the work entrusted to us, and to remain till
the end of the three years. As that cannot.
be, I hope you will bear with me for a time
If I find that I cannot resume my
duties without danger to my health.,
I shall do what every man in my-
position ought to do when so circumstanced—
namely, to give the post up to some other
person who is better able to discharge its
duties. It is a great pleasure to me that
during my absence my place will be taken by
your vice-chairman. From the very first I
have been well supported—l may: say more
than supported—by your vice-chairman, and
his services, have been distinguished by the
utmost zeal and energy. I feel greatly in-
debted to Mr. Reed for the• good feeling and
kindness which induced him to act as he has
acted. I think that the Board has been very
fortunate in having as its vice-chairman sueh
a gentleman as Mr. Reed. (Applause.) He
not only has done his duty towards the Board,
but he has infused the zeal and energy he
himself possesses to so great an extent into
every one of those under him. I thought it
well to take advantage of this opportunity to
have drawn a complete memorandum, showing
what has been done by the Board during the
fifteen months it has been in office. This
document will be read by Mr. Croad, the
clerk to the Board. It shows in a distinct,
and, as I think, a satisfactory form, that the
Board has not alone worked during that

period, but that it has made good progress.
A satisfactory line of future operations has
been laid down which cannot fait to be found
useful. With regard te a motion which has
been placed on the paper respecting the pay-
ment of a salary to the Chairman of the
Board, I have only to say that, so far as I am
concerned, I could on no account consent to
receive a salary as your chairman. I accepted
the office at first without a salary, and, as long
as I remain the chairman, I shall decline to
receive one. But I do not question the pro-
priety of paying your future chairman. It
may be that by attaching a salary to the office
it would induce persons of much ability and
peculiarly fitted for the position to ootne for-
ward, and a great public advantage would be
the result. These are matters which, of course,
the Board would decide for themselves. I re-
fer to the matter, and make the announcement
I have made, because I do not suppose I shall
present at tke next meeting when the ques-
tion may come up for discussion. I wish it
to be understood that I shall not accept any
emolument for my services as chairman; but
as a private member I should probably vote
for the proposition. (Cheers.)
Mr. W. H. Smith, M.P., said that he
believed that he expressed the feeline of every
member of the Board when he said that he
sincerely regretted the necessity which obliged
the chairman to absent himself for a time from
the Board. He begged to thank the noble lord
for his past servioes and his great courtesy on
all occasions to every member, and hoped that
three months hence he would be able to return
to the chairmanship of the Board, fully
restored to health. The noble lord's attention
to the committee meetings of the Board during
the past three months had, no doubt, had a
good deal to do with the fatigue and illness
which he experienced. The Board had there-
fore double cause for regret and esteem fur the
noble lord. (Cheers.)
Mr. Macgregor also expressed regret at the
temporary absence of the noble chairmen.
The Board then adjourned.

articles.title: PEDLARS' ACT.
articles.text:
THE PEDLARS' ACT.

On Tuesday night, at St. Stephen's Mission-
house, Kent-street, Borough, a crowded meet-
ing was held of " hawkers, pedlars, street
dealers, and travelling tradesmen "—or, as
the fraternity are generally designated, of
" eosters "—to form a defence and assistance
association, and to protest against the new and.
tyrannical clauses of the Pedlars' Act, 1871.
Mr. Philip Walter was called to the chair, and
he went through the several obnoxious clauses
of the Act. These were-1, the clause for-
bidding boys under 17 years of age to sell in
the streets, which he considered would inflict
I an incalculable amount of hardship on the
poorest of the poor and an injury on society
in general, as a boy who was prohibited from
earning an honest livelihood would resort to
thieving rather than starve. Another clause
required the payment of ss. before a licence
could be obtained, and numbers of persons,
when, for bare existence, they commenced
selling in the streets, had not that amount in
their possession. Another clause required the
endorsement of a hawker's certificate by the
police-officer of the district in which he
hawked, and as an illnstration of the hard-
ship entailed upon pedlars by this enactment,
he read the written statement of a man
who, last summer, in the Isle of Wight,
was taken; first from Shanklin to Ventnor,
and then to Newport, being looked up for
twenty-three hours, and finally mulcted in
Bs. expenses. He went on to state that he
had communicated with Mr. Bruce, from
whom he had received a reply, stating that
the amendments in the Act were adopted
after great consideration, and. in order to
remedy an almost universal complaint as to
the working of the former Pedlars' Act. The,
new Act bad only been two months in opera-
tion, and until it had been fairly tried
Mr. Bruce could not entertain the question
of altering it. The chairman remarked in
reference to this letter that it was not the first
time Mr. Bruce had refused to receive a depu-
tation, and he called upon the meeting to
take such action as would result in their voice
being heard by Parliament. Mr. W. J. Haynes
then moxed, and Mr. J. Thompson seconded,
a resolution characterizing the Act as: arbitrary,
gruel, and unjust, and otherwise denouncing
it. Mr. J. Robinson moved, and Mr. Griffiths
seconded, a resolutien authorizing the presen-
tation of a petition to Parliament, and the
appointment Of a deputation to wait upon
Mr. Locke and Colonel Beresford, the borough
members. The proceedings, which were con-
ducted in a business-like mannez, closed with
a vote of thanks to the chairman.

PRINTERS' PENSION CORPORATION.

The anniversary festival of this Corporation
was celebrated on Wednesday evening at the
London Tavern; 'Lord G. F. Hamilton in the
chair. Amongst those present were Mr. C.
Reed, M.P. ; Sir J. Bennett, Sheriff; Mr.
Haliburton, Mr. Collingridge, Mr. Gould,
&c. After the usual loyal and constitutional
toasts, the Chairman proposed the toast of
the "Lord Mayor, the Sheriffs, and the
Corporation of the City of London," for
which Sir J. Bennett returned thanks in a
humorous speech. In proposing the toast of
the evening, "The continued, prosperity of
the Printers' Pension, Ahnshouse, and Orphan
Asylum Corporation," the Chairman observed
that the form of the toast greatly pleased him,
for it indicated not merely the prosperity, but
the continued prosperity of the Corporation.
"The report showed that prosperity to be real.
Since the establishment of the Asylum, 340
pensioners had been elected, and 86 were now
receiving its bounty at an annual expenditure
of £1,200. There were 56 applicants now
seeking election, and of these nearly one-half
were over 70 years of age. The almshouse
portion of the institution was, he was glad to
say, in a prosperous condition also, and as a
proof of that the new wing, the foundation-.
stone of which had been laid in 1870, was
opened the year after.- The orphan part of
the institution was the most pleasing of all.
The ;generous contribution of an indi-
vidual enabled them to support the
same number of orphans as before.
The income was now £4,000, the largest ever
received, he believed, by the Corporation.
He was not an advocate for indiseriminate
charity, but when persons supported themselves
and their families up to the age of seventy, he
thought they were worthy of assistance that
could be given to them. The printers had,
he considered, a special claim to support, for
every one must be aware of the toil and
trouble they had to go through in order to
bring out those morning newspapers which
were filled with speeches delivered only a few
hours before they were published. The toast
having been drunk with enthusiasm, Mr. C.
Reed, M.P., proposed the health of the chair-
man, and said that though ho was connected
with many charities there was not one more
worthy of support than the Printers' Pension
Asylum. The printer's brain and body were
both engaged, and he frequently broke down
in middle life. Hence the necessity of such
a charity as this, He regretted that more of
the master printers were not present on the
occasion. The Chairman returned. thanks.
The other toasts of the evening were, "The
Press," "The Stationers' Company," "The '
Authors of England," "The Stewards," and
"This Lathes." The Secretary (Mr. Hodson)
read a list of subscriptions :to the amount of
£357, and a legacy of £642 by Mary Johnson.
The musical arrangements were under the
direction of' Mr. lifontem Smith, assisted by

Lacy.

The railroad business is a good one too. When

TITE'REPOIiT OF THE MEIG2ERA. COM-

MISSION.

The Report of the Meginra Commission was
laid on the table of the House of Commons
on Friday evening. We are enabled, in
anticipation of its distribution to members and
to the public, to give an outline of some of
its chief features. Reviewing the history of
the Megrera, the circumstances in which she
was sent to sea, and in whiehsho was abandoned
off' St. Paul's Island, the Commissioners say,
"We are of opinion that the responsibility
rests on Sir Spencer Robinson, who was Con-
troller from 1861 to 1871. Ist. Practically
he had the power of controlling the opera-
tions carried on in the dockyards, the super-
intendents and dockyard officers being under
his orders. 2nd, The Constructors' depart-.
ment was under his direction." The Com-
missioners premed to indicate the points
in which Sir Spencer Robinson is, in their
view, chargeable with negligence; among
them being insufficient regard to former
reports on the vessel, and the employment of
Spence's cement. From this censure on Sir
Spencer Robinson, Mr. Raillery, one of the
Commissioners, in a long and argumentative
protest, expresses his emphatic dissent; and
the majority of the Commissioners accompany
their blame with a tribute to Sir Spencer's
high character and services, and the frank-
ness of his evidence. The Comnaileioners

think that the Megtora ought not to have
been sent to sea, and attach some blame to
Sir Sydney Dimes in this connection for
disregard of Sir Spencer Robinson's repre-
sentations. They acquit the Admiralty of
fault in ordering the ship to continue her
voyage after the inspection at Queenstown, on
the ground that the defects then reported did
not affect her seaworthiness. They assign as
the cause of the leak which led to her
being stranded the corrosive action of bilge-
water on unprotected iron. Blame in dif-
ferent degrees and connections is assigned
to Mr. E. J. Reed and Mr. Burnaby, to Captain
Luard, Captain Thrupp, Mr. H. Morgan, and
to many dockyard officers and servants. The
dockyard administration in general is un-
favourably reportQd on, as also are some of
the arrangements of the Admiralty, especially
in its Secretarial department. besides the
conclusions, of which we have given the most
important, the report contains a history of
the Megfora, and a narrative of the circum-
stances in which she was sent to sea, and the
incidents of the disastrous voyage.

DEFRAUDING THE AMALGAMATED
COTTON SPINNERS' ASSOCIATION.

At the Hyde Police Court, on Thursday
week, before T. Thornely, Esq., Edward Cross-

ling various sums of money belonging to the
Amalgamated Cotton Spinners' Association.
The prisoner is well-known in the neighbour-
hood, and respectably connected. He is also said
to be possessed of considerable literary abili-
ties, and to have been a frequent contributor
to the Glossop newspapers. He absconded in
January last, when a warrant was taken out
for him, and entrusted to Sergeant Cooper,
who traced him to Halifax, where be was ap-
prehended on Monday last. At the trial,

taken :

. John Clough said: I am a cotton spinner a
Mr. Sidebottom's mill, at Tintwistle, and I am
a member .of the Amalgamated Cotton Spinners'
Association, at Hyde, which embraces our
township. Each cotton spinner at our mill
pays a contribution of ono penny for every day
he works towards the funds of the association.
There are 60 subscribing members out of our
mill. I provide the contribution card marked
"A," which is taken round the mill when the
contributions are collected. I collect for the
bottom room, and then hand the card over to
the prisoner, who reckons up the amount I
have received, after which I hand the money
over to him. The prisoner is a committee man
of the association representing our men, and
ought to enter the names and the amounts paid
over to him in the book produced. His book
ought then to be taken by him to the next
meeting of the association, and what he has
collected be paid over to the money steward. On
the 2nd December last I collected 145., entered
it on the card marked " A," as it now appears,
and handed it over to the prisoner on the fol-
lowing Monday. On the 16th December I
collected 12s. 6th entered it on the same card,
and. handed it over to the prisoner. He filled
the dice of collector more than twelve
months.

Sergeant Cooper said: On Tuesday last I
received the prisoner in custody, he having
been apprehended under a warrant at Halifax,
in Yorkshire. I had the warrant over to him
and told him he was charged with embezzling
various sums of money belonging to the mem-
bers of the Amalgamated Cotton Spinners'
Association. Ho said "I have nothing to
say, only I am willing to pay them the money
back if the committee will come to some
terms.''

The prisoner having been charged in the
usual way, said he had nothing to say.
Ile was then commited for trial on the
chargespreferred against him.

When the hearing of the charge of libel
against Alexander Chaffers was resumed on
Wednesday, Mr. Poland, who has appeared
for the prosecution from the beginning,
announced that Lady Twiss declined to appear

as the alleged libel was concerned, he there-
fore withdrew from the ease. The magistrate,
in discharging the defendant, commented upon
his conduct in the strongest terms, and warned
him not to repeat such frightful tyranny."
As there was another accusation against
Chaffers of having attempted to extort money
from a Mr. Williams by charging him with
bigamy, he was ordered to outer into his
recognizances to appear to the summons on
Thursday morning.

PIECE WORK.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SlR,—Your correspondent" Tyley " alludes
to an article on piece-work, which appeared a
few weeks since, and says the writer has
evidently failed to observe atreat evil which,
in his (Mr. Tyley's) opinion, has tended greatly
to produce much of the bad results complained
of..

Time and space would not allow me to enter
so fully into the subject as to state all the
causes that have produced those ill effects. I am
aware much harm has been done in the manner
suggested, but the system which permits or
encourages the drunkard to enslave himself
that he may earn as much in a few days as the
steady man earns in a week, is a ruinous and
unfair one; and it is more the principle than the
way it is used that is objectionable. I believe
much more harm has been done by the
"avaricious, grasping capitalist," who grinds
men down to the last inch of strength and the
last fraction of money. They, by trying to
make it appear an improvement in the condi-
tion of the workman induce him to take the
work on that principle, and urge him to earn
all the money he can, that it may be seen how,
much he can do in a certain time. Then he
says he is paying too much, and down goes
the pride, and sometimes the workman is put
back to day work; the old slavery stroke
being the standard from which he is expected
to operate.
I have said in my former letter, much may
be urged against piece work socially, and will
quote an argument from an old trade unionist
to prove it--" All raw material is limited,
and :give it to a man to work up by contract,
be will not spare time to make the most of it;
therefore, there is a direet loss to society:"
Again, sir, we have had so many instances in
the building trades of insecurity of construc-
tion, in consequence of the speedy execution of
the work which piece-work has induced,
that society at largo ought to stop it in that
direction at once. I imagine the awful conse-
quence of the axle or wheel of railway car-
riages, plates of boilers, dm., improperly worked
up by the same cause.
I will not trouble you any more now, and
only ask you to publish this in hope
,that it
may be a little more clearly seen that during
the present (i.e., competitive) system of society,
piece-work is wrong in the interests of the
whole community, workmen especially, and
that it signifies but little to the arguments of
my first letter on this subject, who makes it
worse, so long as we prove that the system in
itself is pernicious, as I think myself and Mr.
Tyley has done,—I am, &e._,
GEORGE OLIVER.
Tanners' Unity.

THE CA_USE OF RELIGIOUS HATREDS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sxn,—Why do religious views cause men
to separate from one another, even to making
orthodox believers despise and hate the
unorthodox, and the unorthodox to despise
the orthodox?

The reason is this that the orthodox re-
quire men, whom they style heretics, seeptics,
and unbelievers, to believe creeds, doctrines,
and views •to be good and true, which the
unbelievers thereof hold to be evil and; false.
And the orthodox monopolise the exclusive
use of the name of God, in order to obtain an
infallible authority for exercising the supreme
power of the State to establish their doctrines;
whilst the unorthodox believe it to be a duty
they owe to God to resist such doctrines, as a
foul and gross slander upon God's holy name
and nature. And thus the orthodox and un-
orthodox are at issue with one another as to
what is truth of the orthodox teaching. And
whilst the trial goes on, and the issue is not
either finally or satisfactorily settled, the
orthodox and the unorthodox occupy the
relative positions of the plaintiff end defendant,
with their respective hosts of followers, in
"The great Tiehborne Trial," and the mass,
i.e. the people, occupy the position of a common
jury. And the orthodox seem to be, in the
eyes of the unorthodox, as great impostors
and perjurers as the plaintiff in the Tichborne
trial seems to be in the eyes of the defendant.
And, as in "the Tichborne trial," so in this,
there arc immense estates and interests
dependent upon the result of the trial
and the verdict of the jury; but their
relative positions are reversed, for in the
Tichborne ease the defendants assert that it
is an impostor trying to pat out the true man
who is in possession of the estate; whilst in
the religious trial the unorthodox assert that
impostors and perjurers have obtained posses-
sion, and therefore ought to be turned out
because of having obtained possession by
means of bribery, corruption, intimidation,
and violence, and retaining possession only
through false and forged titles.
The policy of' the orthodox, to effect

and maintain establishment of themselves,
used to be active and: aggressive, with the
view of putting to death such of the un-
orthodox as could not be either bribed over
to their side, or intimidated to be silent; but
the State, refusing to be their "obedient
servant" any longer, to execute and imprison
heretics, the orthodox now are passive, and
oven on their defence, making a merit of
tolerating those whom they cannot silence by
bribery, corruption, intimidation, or persecu-
tion. And meanwhile the trial between the
orthodox and the unorthodox goes on as
though it would never come to an end in our
generation; but "the great Tiohborne trial,"
which was thought would never finish, has
ended, and the views of orthodoxy give great
promise of collapsing in the same manner
for they are daily now being brought to light
through the Press for the people's gaze, to be
examined before .the court of public opinion,
and they seldom pass through that searching
ordeal without being proved to be false and
worthless. And, therefore, the unorthodox
despise the orthodox as either impostors
and perjurers, or the victims and dupes
of impostors and perjurers; whilat the
orthodox hate the unorthodox for unveil-
ing and exposing their doctrines to he
evil and false. And as this religious hatred
divides the nation against itself, destroying
its peace, its patriotism and its unity, and is
owing almost entirely tit the establishment of
evil doctrines and dogmas; therefore, it is the
duty of the
.people, as a common jury, to
express their Judgment (as the jury have done
in the great Tichborne case) upon the views
of the orthodox, in order that the Church may
be at once disestablished as an evil, and false
one, if they refuse to reform it by putting
away its evil and false doctrines. And the
people are as able to judge in this case as the
jury in the groat Tiohborne case, because
the orthodox claimants are almost daily heard
to revile one another as either hypoorites,
impostors, infidels, liars, or wolves in sheep's
clothing, and therefore ought, by their own
testimony, to be disestablished as false
claimants if they refuse to reform by putting
away their real doctrines as false. And it is
the duty aid interest of the people to require
disestablishment, or reform immediately, in
order to remove the chief cause of the religious
hatreds which at present disturb the peace of
almost every faintly, congregation, and city,
throughout the whole nation, owing to the
establishment of evil and false doctrines.
T. G. HEADLEY.
Petersham, S. W.

_

tions to supply all these places. And if the
full force of air is wanted to keep one in good

be expected when it is thus split up? Why,
the chances are twenty to one in favour of
some hundred men some day bang, as usual,

blame? I contend our law-makers will for
not seeing that we have better inspection, and
such things prohibited.
Again, let me say that only about one half
of these have at present begun operations,
yet, at tho same time, already some of the

being to be in, on manyloccasions, Yes, they
are in such a state Sometimes that if you

no air whatever ascending them, but they

bottom, and are each full of gas, and at

charged passes the bottom of these places all
the while, and if a small fire in tho bottom
levels were to take place, it would be a
thousand to one if those said stoppings were
not blown down; and if so, and that body of
gas fired, the whole pit would without a doubt
be blown up. But inspectors know nothing of

Let me ask your readers and the law-
makers if such a course of things is for ever
to be as it is, and we are to continue to be
slain P Again, let me say, that, in a pit like
this one, there are plenty of places that
no butty, chartermaster, or fireman ever
enters before the men in the morning, and if
gas is in they may get it out themselves, and
put their own brattice up as best they can ;
and if a man complains theywill very soon find
a flaw or make one to remove him and send

cause they have had orders from some general
manager not to employ so and so.
When will these unjust law givers let us
have fair play and honest dealings, and these
modern oppressors cease to punish for an
honest, outspoken truth?
Hoping you will pardon the length of this,
letter and insert it in your next issue, I
will close, and beg to subscribe myself,—
Yours respectfully, _

A SILVERDA.LE MINER.

THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE
INDIVIDUAL.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
StR,-:-Before concluding with some general
remarks on what has been advanced on
"Labour and Capital," it is necessary to
allude to another of the essential principles of
harmonic society—the sovereignty of the
individual.

The same (muses that are upheaving thrones
are disturbing the domestic tranquillity of
thousands of families amongst us, Repub.
lioanism, slavery, and the rights of women
are one and the same problem. it is the sole
question of human liberty, or the supremacy
of the individual everywhere and on all
occasions. ,

Every individual particle of matter through-
out the universe possesses within itself certain
principles or laws peculiarly its own, and
when it comes into that precise. position,
and moves in that precise direction which its
own individualities demand, harmony is
evolved. By that means only can natural
classification, natural order, natural organi-
Wien,. natural harmony and agreement be
attained. Every scheme or arrangement which
thwarts the inherent principles of the indi-
vidual atoms, which compose any system or
organisation, is essentially vicious. Objects
bound together contrary to their nature must,
and will seek to reetify themselves by break-
ing the bonds which confine them, while those
that come together by their own attraction
remain quiescent and content. Individuality
is a principle which pervades universal nature
and gives rise to infinite diversity.
Human system builders should begin to die-
cover the universal truth of individuality.
Every attempt to adjust the capacities of' one
human being, his adaptations, his wants, or
his responsibilities by the capacities, the adap-
tations, the wants, or the responsibilities of'
another human being, except in the very
broadest generalities is unqualifiedly futile
and hopeless. If such builders are unable to
see clearly how all.external restrictions can be
removed with safety to the well-being of
society, let them, nevertheless, not abandon a
principle ; which is self-evident. At all,
hazards, on all occasions this individuality
must be recognised and indulged, because it is,
infinite and cannot be measured or prescribed
for; it is inherent and cannot be conquered; it
is the essential element of order, and cannot
consequently be infringed without engender-•
ing infinite confusion such as has universally'.
reigned in the administration of human
aflitirs.

,
The atoms of which society is composed are
the individual men and women in it. In
order, therefore, that society may be harmonic,
the individuals must be so disposed of that
the destiny of each shall be controlled by hia
own, individualities of taste, conscience, in
' -
oapaeities and ,will. Each one and.
no one else knows the determining force of his,
own attractions, No one, therefore, can de-
cide for him. fleece individuality, as regards
every member of the human family, can be-
come the law of human action only by securing
to each individual the sovereign determination
of his own judgment and of his Own conduct
in all things.
This is what is meant by the supremacy or
the sovereignty of the individual; and thu.
sovereignty is limited only by the ever accom-
panying condition, resulting from the savc..
reignty of others, that the disagreeable conse-
quences of his own action be assumed by
himself. What each sovereign does must be
at his own cost ; he must not throw the bur-
densoine consequences of his action on others;
and thus at at their cost.

Government of all sorts is adverse to free-
dom. it destroys the freedom of the subject,
directly, by virtue of the faot that he is a
Subject, and destroys equally, the freedom of
the governor, indire‘tly, by tleyolying on hint

the necessity of overlooking and attempting,
hopelessly, to regulate the conduct of others
—a task never yet accomplished, and the
attempt at which is sufficiently harassing to
wear the life out of the most zealous advocate of
order. With the greater devplopnaent of the
individuals to be governed the task becomes
proportionally more onerous, until, in our day,
the business of governing grows vulgar from
its excessive laboriousness.
_ _

_
We must hail the progress of that unspar-
ing Criticism of old institutions, which is
the characteristic of the present ' age. Upon
sifting Protestantism, Democracy and So-
cialism, we find they are merely different
expressions of the same idea, are identical in
the assertion of the supremacy of the indi-
vidual, a dogma essentially revolutionary and
antagonistic to the basis principle of all the older
institutions of Society, which make the indi-
vidual subordinate and subject to the Church,
to the State, and to 'Society respectively.
This sovereignty of the individual is sub-
stantially the whole of the present restless
reformatory movements, It is the vital energy,
the living soul itself of them.
Protestants may differ from each other
without ceasing to be Protestants' so long as
they assert the paramount right of private or
individual judgment in matters of conscience.
It is that only which makes them Protestants,
and distinguishes them , from the Catholic
world, which asserts, on the contrary, the
supreme authority of the Church. In like
manner deinoorats may differ from eaoh other
and still remain 'democrats, so long as they
maintain the one essential principle and
condition of democracy, that all governmental
powers reside in the people, or are only
delegated by the people, ' and can at any
moment be resumed by them, that is, by the
individuals. It is this dogma, and this alone,
which makes the democrat, and distinguishes
him from the despot fat, or the defender of the
divine right of kings.
Socialism assumes every shade and variety of
opinion respecting the modes of realising its
own aspirations, but always asserts the para.-
mount right of the individual over social
institutions, consequently that all existing
social institutions shall be so modified that
the individual shall be in no manner sob-
jected to them ; that society shall be so reor-
ganised that every individual shall be enforced
to (loose and vary his own destiny, condition,
or pursuits in life' untrammelled by social
restrictions, so that every man may be a la*
unto himself paramount to all other human
laws, and the sole judge for himself of the
divine and of the requisitions of his own indi-
stidual nature and 'organisation. Socialism
demands therefore' the emancipation of the
individual from social; bondage by whatso-
ever moans will 'effect that design, in the same '
manner as Protestantism demands the eman-
cipation of the individual from ecclesiastical
bondage, and democracy from politisal. ;
The 'sole bads on which the supremacy of
the individiial can rest is equity—the rendering
to each that which is his own. Without such a
basis the dogma that each individual is a
soVereign is an ttbstraot principle, but wholly
inotipabio of realisation. The individual
sovereign is so of right, bat not so really. Ho
is a saviereign'without dominions, treated ' as a
pretender, and his claim 'ridiculed by the
actual incumbent. The assertion of sovereignty
is a phantom and a delusion until the sovereign
anises, to his own. The cost principle, as the
essential element or equity, gives to e,aeh his
own, whit+ nothing else can. It places all in
a conditionof independence, and dissolves the
relation of protectors and protected by render-
ing protection unnecessary. ' • .
It' hoe been the function Of *titers and
preachers npon morals 'hitherto, to incubate '
the ditty of submitting to the exigencies of
false; soeial • relations ; but knowledge, on the
otherhand, teaches the reetifteatiOn of those'
relations themselves. So long as men find
themselves enibarassed by complicated cenned-
tion of interests, so that the consequences of
their acts inevitably devolve, upon others, the
highest virtue comosts in mutual concessions
and abrt• egatiOns of Selfhood, Renee, to enforce
the'reltiotant sacrifice, the necesSity for strin-
gent appeals • to the conscience. The truest
condition of society, however, is that in which
each individual is enabled and constrained to
assume, to the greatest extent possible, the cost
or disagreeable consequences of his own act. That
condition of society can only arise from a osasial
disintegration or interests--front rene'doring •
the interest of all' LIS Completely individual as
their person. This would seem to be iri
exact antagonism to association and the views
of socialisni of all the isarions schools; hut by
avoiding combinations of interests the benefits'
of co-operation and the economies of the large
scale need not be lost. Dy combinations are
meant partnership interats and community of
property and administration, such as confuses,
in a degree, or obliterates the lines of indivi-
duality in the ownership or use of property.
fly co-operation is meant such an arrangement
of the property and itidtistiial interestg of the
different individuals of the community that
each, in pursaing. his own pleasitro and
benefit contributes incidentally to the pleasure
or benefit of the others.
It must not
.be supposed, that disconnection
of interests implies m the slightest degree an

isolation of persons. A hundred or a thousand
men may be engaged in the same shop-, and
still their interests be entirely individualised.
Such is the case now under the present wages
system. The labourers in a manufacturing
establishment, for example, have no common
interest, no partnership, no combined responsi-
bilities. Their interests are completely in-
dividualised, and yet They work together.
This is all right. It is not at this point that
the evil lurks which the socialist seeks or
should seek to remedy. These men and
women co-operate completely in their labour.
They all work at distinct functions, to a
common end, which 'is do-operation. • The
evil to be remedied is neither in their indivi-
duality of interests nor in any want of co-
operation. It is solely in the want of
mutuality in the results of that co-operation—
in
.other words in the want of equity—in the
want of a regulating principle, which would
secure to each°the full legitimate results of his
own labour. The difficulty is that the whole
hundred or the - whole thousand Men now
labour and co;.operate, not for their own
benefit, but for the benefit of one—the
employer. Under the cost principle their
interests will be individual 'as they are now;
.they will co-operate as they do now, or rather
more perfectly, but they will co-operate for
their own mutual benefit—the employer, or
chief receiving, like ell others,- merely the.
equivalent or reward of his oitii labour.
W. Am Nub.

EMIGRATION.
To the Editor of .the BEE-HisE.

was gratified by the Times report of,
and leading article on, the conversatiori in
the House of Commons on Tuesday regarding
tho alienising of so many of the Queen s most
valuable subjects, through emigration to the
United • States of America. Rapid and ao-
curate as is the transmission of reports of
proceedings in Parliament by means of the
telegraph, generally it is too brief to be antis-
tory. In the present instance I regret to
find it has been misleading. To this cause I
attribute an erroneous view that is taken in
Scotland and Ireland, as evinced by leading
articles in three newspapers now before me.
These articles have been written on the
assumption that on the occasion referred to I
supported emigration at the expense of the•
State, and transportation of paupers. I did
neither. What, in common with a growing
number of patriotic and philanthropic persons,
I desire is diversion, by cheapened or gratuitous
land, by, in the case of the more distant
colonies, facilitated and accelerated transit,
and by better adapted; law and bUsiness
arrangements, of the actual spontaneous
exodus, from its present destination (which
involves inestimable and irreparable loss to
the. Empire) into some of the unoccupied tracts
of British soil which superabound in North
America, in Africa, and in Australia.
Contrary to a prevailing impression, in the
two latter Continual- many millions of acres
of arable land are still under the &treat control of
the Crown. As to the yet greater number of
millions which have ,been absolutely trans-
ferred to the control of certain Colonies,'
colonial interests appear to coincide with
Imperial considerations of the utmost weight
and urgency in demanding. 6-operation be-
tween the Legislatures and Governments Of
the Colonies and those of the Mother Country
for the object, so beneficial to all concerned,
of peopleing ond reclaiming and enriching
British territories. This is surely a principal
part of our nation's mission. Why., if not
for this great end, have we received, and do
we hold, so noble a trust as the administra-
tion of about one-half of the waste lands of the.
globe? I atn glad to learn that among the
Colonial agents the proceedings of Tuesday
have been viewed with satisfaction. ' The
working population at home will certainly not
allow the 'question now stirred to drop. It
is the duty, and within the pewer, of our
characteristically earnest Government to do
much but at present they (not to. say the
nation') giVe forth neither declaration nor
manifestation of a positive policy in the
matter. Drifting despair, one may say, of
success if they wore to avow a policy Con-.
servative of the Empire, marks their course.
The Opposition front benches are not, any-
wise, .more demonstrative. All this tends to
that new fusion, that combined action for the
maintenance of the Empire and of popular
rights, whieli increasing confusion and in-
action rn other departments of statesmanship
seems to encourage 'loyal,' hopeful, and re-
solute subjects of the Crown without respect
to transient party politics, to look for, as sooll.
as that barrier Of separation, non-recognition
of the Church question as an open one, is
removed out of the way.—l am, Sir, your
faithful servant,

R. A. MACVIE.
Reading Rooms, House of Commons.

MEETING IN HYDE PARK AGAINST

THE PARKS BILL.

The agitators who have found an opportunity
for the exercise of their vocation in denouncing
the measure now before Parliament for plaeing
the Royal Parks under similar regulations to
those that are applied to every other park in
the kingdom, continued the agitation on Sun-
day by a "demonstration." Mr. Odger was the
chairman at one stand; while at two others it
Was stated that Mr. Hennessey and Mr.
Riddle would be the chairmen, Mr. Bradlaugh
moving the resolution. The proceedings were
identical at all three stands, and therefore a
brief description of what took place under the
direction of Ni'. Odger will suffice for all.
The Chairman denounced the Parks Regula-
tion Bill as a "vile and odious" measure
Which they had come into the Park to burn as
a mark of• their profound contempt for the
tyrannical so-called Liberal Government,
which had got into power through the aid of
the working classes only to turn round on
their friends and do the dirty work of the
Tories. After a few other propositions of an
equally accurate description, he called on Mr.
Shiptop, to move a resolution:

Thit this meeting, consisting of repre-
sentatives of various political ana social
organised bodies, as well as of persons of all
eludes of political opinion, denounce the
Parks Bill, introduced into the House of
Commons by Mr. Ayrton on behalf of the
Government, as a gross outrage on the con-
stitutional, time-secured, and altogether indis-
putable right of the people to the free use of
the national parks for the purpose of public
meeting and free speech; and that this
meeting, feeling convinced that the conduct
of the Government, in bringing forward such a
measure, has been prompted by the meanest
and vilest Motives—to deceive its friends and
to do the dirty work of its opponents, hoping
thereby to lengthen its term of office, which
is every day becoming more and more a re-
proaoh to a presumably free and progressive
country; this meeting feeling also that words
fail to express the contempt, disgust, and
indignation which this attempt at Algerian
legislation has produced, resolve that this bill
be publicly burnt in this very park, which it
isintended so misehibvously and so insidiously
to filch from its rightful owners, the people
therefore instruct the chairman to set it on fire
at MOO."

This resolution having boon duly seconded
